Initiative_Name: Adopt a net-zero buildings plan
Description: Set the portfolio baseline, target pathway, technology sequence, governance, budget envelope and review cadence for buildings. This is a portfolio plan, not a substitute for individual measures.
Why_Benefit: Hospitality estates are energy-intensive, operate long hours and renew assets in recurring cycles. A costed portfolio plan sequences measures around refurbishments and replacements, reduces stranded capex and gives operators a credible path for investors, clients and customers.
How_Text: 1) Define ownership/lease boundary. 2) Baseline energy, refrigerants and capex cycles. 3) Model measure bundles and dependencies. 4) Approve annual portfolio roadmap. 5) Refresh with measured performance.
KPI: % of controlled floor area covered by an approved, costed pathway; % of annual pathway actions delivered on time; forecast portfolio tCO2e variance to pathway
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Experiential Leisure; Contract Caterers only where delegated asset/capital control is documented
Sector_Not_Included: Exclude sites where the operator does not control the relevant asset, utility, specification or capital decision.
Source_Old_Initiative: Adopt a net-zero buildings plan

Initiative_Name: Measure and verify building energy performance
Description: Establish adjusted baselines and compare post-implementation energy, cost and carbon performance with forecast outcomes. Meter installation and BEMS control remain separate initiatives.
Why_Benefit: Thin margins and changing occupancy, trading hours and weather can make projected savings difficult to trust. Normalised measurement verifies which projects actually reduce bills and carbon, strengthens future investment cases and protects supplier performance guarantees.
How_Text: Define baseline period and adjustment variables; record meter boundaries; verify installation; compare like-for-like post-period data; investigate variance; lock the approved result and evidence trail.
KPI: % of completed measures with an approved baseline and 12-month verification; verified annual kWh, £ and tCO2e saving; forecast-to-realised saving variance (%)
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Exclude sites without sufficient interval or billing data until a baseline can be established.

Initiative_Name: Optimise and upgrade HVAC systems and controls
Description: Follow a repair-before-replace pathway: recommission sensors, valves, actuators, setpoints and sequencing to restore intended HVAC performance; replace chillers, air-handling units or packaged plant only where equipment is end-of-life, unreliable, incorrectly sized or materially less efficient than suitable modern alternatives.
Why_Benefit: A staged HVAC approach protects guest comfort and operational continuity while avoiding premature capital replacement. Recommissioning removes control-related waste at relatively low cost, while planned replacement of inefficient or unreliable plant can reduce energy exposure, emergency capex and service disruption.
How_Text: Survey plant, controls, loads and fault history; correct sensor, valve and sequencing faults first; compare continued repair, recommissioning and replacement; right-size and procure efficient plant where justified; commission and verify comfort, ventilation and energy performance.
KPI: % of eligible HVAC capacity recommissioned or upgraded; seasonal plant efficiency (COP, SCOP or boiler efficiency); weather-adjusted HVAC kWh and tCO2e saved; comfort complaints or hours outside setpoint
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Experiential Leisure; Contract Caterers only where delegated asset/capital control is documented
Sector_Not_Included: Exclude sites where the operator does not control the relevant asset, utility, specification or capital decision.
Source_Old_Initiative: Install energy efficient HVAC systems

Initiative_Name: Install smart draught beverage dispense systems
Description: Replace standard draught lines with a closed, continuously cooled keg-to-tap system combining insulated product lines, secondary gas control, foam management, efficient cooling and scheduled professional cleaning. The system maintains consistent beer and cider temperature, reduces fobbing and extends line-cleaning intervals from weekly to every 6–12 weeks.
Why_Benefit: Beer, water, dispense gas and cleaning chemicals are lost during line cleaning, while temperature hot spots increase foam, waste and inconsistent serves. Smart dispense systems reduce these losses, release staff time, improve saleable yield and protect drink quality and repeat sales.
How_Text: Measure draught volume, taps, cleaning frequency, wastage and cellar energy; select a cellar-, bar- or underbar system; survey line routes and cooling; install insulated cooled lines, controls and compatible dispense equipment; train staff on keg changes, hygiene and perfect-pour routines; move to supplier-managed 6- or 12-week cleaning; track yield, water, energy, quality and sales.
KPI: Saleable draught yield (% of keg volume); cleaning loss (pints/tap/year) and cleaning labour (hours/tap/year); cellar cooling kWh/tap; sales £/tap and dispense-quality complaints
Sector_Included: Pubs, bars and breweries; restaurants, hotels, experiential leisure and contract caterers operating draught beer or cider
Sector_Not_Included: Sites without draught beer or cider service, including most QSR; concession sites without control of dispense equipment
Source_Old_Initiative: Implement Smart Dispense Systems

Initiative_Name: Install timer controls across eligible equipment
Description: Use plug-in timers, fused-spur timers, run-back timers, time clocks or BMS schedules to match equipment operation to trading hours and real demand. Suitable applications include domestic hot water, space heating, kitchen extraction, cellar remote coolers, pool and whirlpool blowers or pumps, exterior and back-of-house lighting, dishwashers, glasswashers, cutlery polishers, coffee machines, vending and other ancillary plug loads. Controls should retain required pre-heat, post-run and manual-boost periods.
Why_Benefit: A low-cost control measure that removes out-of-hours energy use without replacing serviceable equipment. It can reduce utility bills and emissions quickly, standardise opening and closing routines across sites, and provide a scalable first step before higher-capex equipment upgrades.
How_Text: Inventory equipment and operating hours; identify avoidable out-of-hours runtime; classify critical and timer-eligible loads; select controls with the correct load rating and switching arrangement; pilot schedules against service needs; retain pre-heat, post-run and manual override; verify food temperatures, hot-water hygiene, ventilation and guest comfort; monitor overrides and roll out successful settings across the estate.
KPI: % of eligible equipment under automatic time control; out-of-hours runtime and kWh by equipment category; annual £ and tCO2e saving; override or exception rate
Sector_Included: Restaurants; QSR; pubs, bars and breweries; contract caterers with control of site equipment; hotels; experiential leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Life-safety, security and IT systems; food-storage refrigeration compressors without validated smart controls; 24/7 guest-critical loads; equipment without a safe shutdown sequence or asset-control rights
Source_Old_Initiative: Install timer controls on domestic hot-water boilers; Roll out equipment timers across boilers, refrigeration and kitchen equipment

Initiative_Name: Optimise fans and pumps with variable-speed drives, efficient motors and demand controls
Description: Fit high-efficiency motors and variable-speed drives to eligible fans and pumps, and add temperature, optical, air-quality or flow sensing where commercial kitchen extract and make-up air should follow cooking demand. This is a component and controls measure, not whole-HVAC replacement.
Why_Benefit: Fans, pumps and kitchen extract often run at peak output despite variable hospitality demand. Matching motor and ventilation output to actual load reduces electricity, mechanical wear, noise and conditioned-air losses without compromising ventilation, circulation, food safety or customer comfort.
How_Text: Profile fan and pump load and run hours; identify throttle/damper control and kitchen demand patterns; verify motor, hood and fire-safety compatibility; install VSDs, efficient motors and sensors; balance extract/make-up air and tune minimum speeds; commission across operating modes; verify kWh and service performance.
KPI: % of eligible variable-load motor kW under VSD or efficient-motor control; % of eligible kitchens with demand-controlled ventilation; fan and pump kWh per operating hour; annual kWh and tCO2e saved
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure; kitchen demand controls apply only where commercial kitchens and relevant asset/control rights exist
Sector_Not_Included: Fixed-speed or process-critical loads where compatibility, duty profile or run hours do not support variable control; sites without commercial kitchens for DCKV; sites where the operator cannot modify ventilation or motor controls.
Source_Old_Initiative: Use intelligent kitchen extract systems

Initiative_Name: Recover and reuse waste heat from refrigeration, cooking or wastewater
Description: Capture useful heat from process refrigeration, cooking or wastewater and transfer it to a coincident hot-water or space-heating load. Ventilation heat recovery is excluded.
Why_Benefit: Hospitality sites frequently reject heat from refrigeration, cooking or wastewater while simultaneously buying energy for hot water or space heating. Recovering this heat lowers boiler or electric demand, reduces plant stress and improves the value of existing equipment.
How_Text: Map heat sources and temperature; map coincident heat sinks; model seasonal match; design heat exchanger/storage; protect hygiene; meter heat delivered and displaced fuel.
KPI: Recovered heat delivered (kWhth/year); useful-heat utilisation (% of available recovered heat); displaced gas or electricity kWh and £; tCO2e avoided
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Sites without a stable heat source and coincident heat demand, or without asset/pipework control.
Source_Old_Initiative: Recover and reuse commercial heat

Initiative_Name: Upgrade boiler burner controls and balance heat-distribution systems
Description: Improve retained boiler performance through burner/combustion controls, turndown, hydraulic balancing, pipe insulation and maintenance. Excludes boiler replacement and generic HVAC scheduling.
Why_Benefit: Retained gas boilers commonly cycle and operate inefficiently at part load. Better burner control and balanced distribution reduce fuel waste and breakdown risk while extracting more value from assets that are not yet due for replacement.
How_Text: Complete combustion and distribution survey; measure excess air/cycling; balance circuits; upgrade compatible controls; insulate exposed distribution; recommission and verify gas use.
KPI: Combustion efficiency (%); boiler starts or cycles per operating hour; heat-distribution temperature or balance variance; weather-adjusted gas kWh, £ and tCO2e saved
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Experiential Leisure; Contract Caterers only where delegated asset/capital control is documented
Sector_Not_Included: Exclude sites where the operator does not control the relevant asset, utility, specification or capital decision.
Source_Old_Initiative: Use gas boiler additives

Initiative_Name: Upgrade domestic hot-water generation, storage and circulation controls
Description: Reduce hot-water energy through efficient generation, insulated storage/pipework, demand-based circulation and appropriate temperature control. Space heating and cooking are excluded.
Why_Benefit: Hotels, leisure venues and catering operations use large volumes of hot water and can lose energy through storage and continuous circulation. Better generation and circulation control reduce fuel and pump costs while protecting hygiene and hot-water availability.
How_Text: Meter or estimate hot-water load; inspect storage and distribution; address leaks/insulation; optimise circulation; select efficient replacement plant; verify hygiene temperatures and energy.
KPI: Hot-water energy intensity (kWh/guest-night, cover or litre delivered); storage and circulation loss (%); circulation-pump runtime or kWh; annual £ and tCO2e saved
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Experiential Leisure; Contract Caterers only where delegated asset/capital control is documented
Sector_Not_Included: Exclude sites where the operator does not control the relevant asset, utility, specification or capital decision.

Initiative_Name: Automate shutdown of non-HVAC, non-lighting equipment outside operating hours
Description: Use timers, smart relays or programmable controls to switch eligible small-power and operational equipment off when not needed. Lighting and HVAC controls are excluded.
Why_Benefit: Kitchen, bar, office and guest-service equipment is often left running after trading. Automated shutdown reduces persistent baseload across many low-cost control points, improves site margins and makes closing procedures more consistent.
How_Text: Profile half-hourly baseload; identify safe controllable loads; define schedules and overrides; install controls; train staff; verify out-of-hours demand reduction.
KPI: % of eligible loads under automated shutdown; out-of-hours baseload kW and kWh; annual £ and tCO2e saving; manual override or exception rate
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Safety-critical, food-safety, refrigeration, life-safety or continuously required loads.
Source_Old_Initiative: Install equipment timers

Initiative_Name: Implement power management for small-power, IT and server-room equipment
Description: Apply device sleep settings, server consolidation, efficient uninterruptible power supplies, correctly sized cooling and managed shutdown to IT and other operator-controlled electrical loads.
Why_Benefit: POS systems, office devices, displays, network equipment and local servers can create a continuous electrical and cooling load. Power management cuts unnecessary 24-hour consumption and improves control of IT assets without affecting trading availability.
How_Text: Inventory devices and run hours; measure baseload; enable power-management policy; consolidate/retire equipment; optimise UPS and cooling; verify kWh.
KPI: % of managed devices with sleep or shutdown policy enabled; out-of-hours IT and small-power kWh; kWh per workstation or site; server-room PUE where applicable
Sector_Included: Hotels, larger Restaurants/QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Contract Caterers and Experiential Leisure with material managed IT loads
Sector_Not_Included: Sites with only negligible or landlord-controlled IT loads.

Initiative_Name: Upgrade lift and escalator drives and controls
Description: Improve operator-controlled vertical transport through efficient drives, regenerative braking where viable, sleep/standby controls and optimised operating schedules.
Why_Benefit: Lifts and escalators are essential to accessibility and guest movement in hotels and multi-storey leisure venues. Efficient drives and standby controls reduce electricity and peak demand while improving reliability, ride quality and service continuity.
How_Text: Obtain controller/drive data and run profiles; assess standby and regeneration; prioritise controls before replacement; procure compliant upgrade; verify kWh and service quality.
KPI: Lift or escalator kWh per trip or operating hour; standby energy share (%); % of eligible units using sleep or regeneration; annual kWh, £ and tCO2e saved
Sector_Included: Hotels, Experiential Leisure and multi-storey hospitality sites with controlled lifts/escalators
Sector_Not_Included: Single-storey sites and landlord-controlled vertical transport.

Initiative_Name: Optimise swimming-pool circulation, heating, covers and backwashing
Description: Reduce operator-controlled pool energy and water demand through covers, variable-speed circulation, efficient heating, optimised backwashing and safe temperature management.
Why_Benefit: Swimming pools are among the most energy- and water-intensive hospitality amenities. Optimising covers, circulation, heating and backwashing protects the guest offer while reducing pumping, evaporation, heating and water-treatment costs.
How_Text: Submeter pool plant; review filtration/turnover and backwash; assess covers; optimise pump speed and schedules; review temperatures with safety team; verify energy and water.
KPI: Pool energy intensity (kWh/m² water surface or per bather); circulation-pump kWh; make-up and backwash water litres per bather; annual £ and tCO2e saved
Sector_Included: Hotels and Experiential Leisure with swimming pools
Sector_Not_Included: All sites without pools; landlord-controlled pool plant.

Initiative_Name: Replace high-GWP refrigerants with lower-GWP alternatives during planned plant intervention
Description: Move eligible refrigeration and cooling plant from high-GWP refrigerants to technically safe lower-GWP alternatives at replacement or major service points.
Why_Benefit: Refrigeration and cooling are essential to hospitality operations, and leaked high-GWP refrigerant can be a major direct-emissions source. A planned transition reduces climate and regulatory exposure, improves refrigerant availability resilience and avoids rushed equipment decisions.
How_Text: Build equipment/charge inventory; rank by charge × GWP × leakage; assess alternatives and safety class; plan conversion/replacement; recover old gas; update records and verify energy.
KPI: % of in-scope refrigerant charge converted to lower-GWP alternatives; charge-weighted average GWP; kg of high-GWP refrigerant retired; lifecycle leakage risk reduced (tCO2e)
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Equipment where the alternative is unsafe, unlawful or incompatible without full replacement.

Initiative_Name: Install refrigerant leak detection and implement rapid repair
Description: Use fixed or portable detection, alarms and a defined response process to find and repair refrigerant leakage earlier.
Why_Benefit: Refrigerant leaks increase recharge cost, equipment energy use and failure risk, with potential consequences for food stock, guest comfort and trading continuity. Early detection shortens the time to repair and reduces emissions, maintenance cost and product-loss risk.
How_Text: Map charge and statutory thresholds; establish baseline leakage; select detection method; set alarm/escalation; train contractors; log leak, repair and recharge data.
KPI: Annual refrigerant leakage rate (% of installed charge); median alarm-to-repair time; kg of refrigerant lost or recharged; tCO2e leakage avoided
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Equipment with no refrigerant charge or outside the operator's maintenance control.

Initiative_Name: Maintain a governed refrigerant inventory and leakage record
Description: Maintain asset-level refrigerant type, charge, location, ownership, service, leakage and end-of-life status to support compliance and abatement prioritisation.
Why_Benefit: Large estates and outsourced maintenance can leave operators without reliable refrigerant charge and leakage data. A governed inventory supports compliance, exposes high-GWP and high-leak assets and directs maintenance and replacement capital to the greatest risks.
How_Text: Define asset ID and ownership; collect nameplate/service records; reconcile charge and top-ups; calculate annual leakage; flag missing records/high-risk assets; audit annually.
KPI: % of in-scope assets with verified refrigerant type, charge, ownership and service history; % of total charge covered by leakage data; % of high-risk assets with an approved action plan
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Equipment demonstrably outside the reporting and maintenance boundary.

Initiative_Name: Recover refrigerants at equipment end of life and document transfer
Description: Recover, contain and transfer refrigerants for reclamation or destruction during equipment decommissioning rather than venting or unmanaged disposal.
Why_Benefit: Hospitality equipment is regularly replaced during kitchen, refrigeration and HVAC renewal. Documented refrigerant recovery prevents high-impact end-of-life emissions, demonstrates compliant contractor control and protects the organisation from unmanaged disposal liabilities.
How_Text: Include recovery in decommissioning scope; record pre-work charge; use certified contractor; weigh recovered gas; obtain waste/transfer documentation; close asset record.
KPI: % of decommissioned refrigerant charge recovered; kg transferred for reclamation or destruction; % of disposals with complete transfer evidence; end-of-life tCO2e avoided
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Equipment outside the organisation's decommissioning or procurement control.

Initiative_Name: Upgrade refrigeration equipment, doors, seals, fans and controls
Description: Improve cold-storage energy performance through efficient equipment, EC fans, doors/lids, seals, insulation, defrost and control optimisation. Refrigerant GWP and leakage are separate.
Why_Benefit: Refrigeration operates continuously and directly protects food safety, beverage quality and product availability. Efficient cabinets, doors, seals, fans and controls reduce one of the largest controllable electricity loads while lowering spoilage, maintenance and failure risk.
How_Text: Meter representative cabinets/plant; inspect seals, doors, fans, defrost and setpoints; repair low-cost defects; compare ETL products; replace at end-of-life; verify kWh.
KPI: Refrigeration electricity intensity (kWh/m³ refrigerated volume or per cover); door, seal and defrost exception rate; annual kWh, £ and tCO2e saved; product-loss incidents
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Landlord- or supplier-owned equipment without operator upgrade authority.

Initiative_Name: Adopt a validated warmer freezer setpoint where product and food-safety rules allow
Description: Raise freezer setpoints only for product categories and equipment validated for the change, with documented food-safety, quality and contractual approval.
Why_Benefit: Freezers run continuously, so even a small validated setpoint change can reduce annual electricity with little or no capex. The measure offers low-disruption savings where product quality, food safety requirements and equipment specifications permit.
How_Text: Identify eligible products/equipment; secure technical and food-safety approval; pilot temperature stability and quality; adjust setpoint; monitor alarms and kWh; scale only after validation.
KPI: % of eligible freezer load operating at the approved warmer setpoint; freezer kWh per m³ or tonne of product; annual kWh, £ and tCO2e saved; temperature or product-quality exceptions
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Products/equipment requiring colder temperatures or lacking technical and food-safety approval.
Source_Old_Initiative: Switch freezer temperatures to -15.

Initiative_Name: Phase out fossil-fuelled patio heaters and avoid unnecessary outdoor heating
Description: Eliminate outdoor heating where possible; where a justified customer need remains, assess targeted zonal electric infrared only after demand reduction and control.
Why_Benefit: Fossil patio heaters consume significant energy to provide a non-core service in an exposed area. Removing unnecessary heating or using targeted alternatives reduces fuel cost and emissions while retaining outdoor trading where it has clear customer value.
How_Text: Inventory heaters/fuel/run hours; challenge service need; improve shelter/blankets/controls; remove fossil units; if retained service is justified, trial targeted electric zoning; verify net energy.
KPI: Number and rated capacity of fossil patio heaters removed; annual fuel kWh and operating hours avoided; annual £ and tCO2e saved; outdoor-area sales or customer complaints during trial
Sector_Included: Restaurants, Pubs/Bars/Breweries and Hotels with outdoor trading areas
Sector_Not_Included: Sites without outdoor heating or without authority over the equipment/energy.
Source_Old_Initiative: Avoid outdoor patio heaters, or if you must use them, use infra-red electric heaters

Initiative_Name: Conduct whole-life carbon assessments for major capital projects
Description: Assess product, construction, use-stage and end-of-life carbon for major construction, refurbishment and fit-out projects using consistent boundaries and data hierarchy.
Why_Benefit: Hospitality businesses refurbish and refit sites frequently, so operational energy alone can overlook substantial construction and material impacts. Whole-life carbon assessment identifies the design choices that drive carbon and cost before they become difficult to change.
How_Text: Set the project threshold; define the baseline option; quantify materials and operational scenarios using the RICS life-cycle modules; use environmental product declarations where available; test options; update the assessment at approval stages and completion.
KPI: % of major projects assessed at concept, design and completion; whole-life carbon intensity (kgCO2e/m²); reduction versus baseline option (% and tCO2e); design-to-completion assessment variance
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Minor works below the organisation's approved materiality threshold.

Initiative_Name: Set operational-energy and embodied-carbon targets for new construction and major refurbishment
Description: Set measurable operational-energy and upfront/whole-life-carbon targets at project brief stage, using consistent project type and life-cycle boundaries.
Why_Benefit: New sites and major refurbishments lock in energy performance and material choices for many years. Clear operational and embodied-carbon targets give designers and suppliers accountable thresholds, reducing performance gaps and expensive future retrofit requirements.
How_Text: Select peer benchmark and project boundary; set operational and embodied targets; allocate targets to design team; include in employer's requirements; track at each stage.
KPI: % of projects with approved operational-energy and embodied-carbon targets before concept approval; target kWh/m² and kgCO2e/m²; % of projects forecast to meet target at each design gate
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Experiential Leisure; Contract Caterers only where delegated asset/capital control is documented
Sector_Not_Included: Exclude sites where the operator does not control the relevant asset, utility, specification or capital decision.
Source_Old_Initiative: When undertaking new construction projects, design for performance and set embodied carbon targets

Initiative_Name: Apply carbon criteria at capital-project investment and design gates
Description: Require project teams to demonstrate performance against approved carbon targets before funding, design freeze, procurement and completion decisions.
Why_Benefit: Hospitality brands often repeat approved designs across many locations. Carbon criteria at investment and design gates prevent high-impact options from being committed and avoid multiplying poor material or energy decisions across the estate.
How_Text: Add carbon deliverables to gate checklist; define accountable approver; require baseline/options/variance; record decision and conditions; verify completion against approval.
KPI: % of investment and design gates with complete carbon evidence; forecast tCO2e change arising from gate decisions; % of conditional approvals with actions closed before the next gate
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Experiential Leisure; Contract Caterers only where delegated asset/capital control is documented
Sector_Not_Included: Exclude sites where the operator does not control the relevant asset, utility, specification or capital decision.

Initiative_Name: Require EPDs or product-specific carbon data for priority materials and equipment
Description: Collect comparable product carbon data for high-impact materials and capital equipment so procurement and WLCA can compare like-for-like options.
Why_Benefit: Repeated procurement across common materials and equipment can create a significant aggregate footprint. Comparable EPD and product data allow buyers to distinguish genuinely lower-carbon options, use purchasing scale and support credible customer and corporate reporting.
How_Text: Define priority categories; specify accepted standards and expiry; request EPDs in tender; validate declared unit/modules; store source/version; link selected product to project calculation.
KPI: % of priority spend and material mass covered by valid product-specific EPD or LCA data; % of records with matched declared unit and life-cycle modules; average data-quality score
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Low-materiality purchases outside the approved priority list.

Initiative_Name: Prioritise refurbishment, reuse and adaptation before new construction
Description: Evaluate whether existing buildings, structures and fit-outs can meet the need through retention or adaptation before approving demolition and new construction.
Why_Benefit: Hotels, pubs and restaurants often refresh concepts before the building structure reaches end of life. Retaining and adapting viable assets can reduce demolition, new-material demand, planning risk, closure time and capital cost while preserving established locations.
How_Text: Define service need; survey existing asset; model retain/refurbish/new-build options; compare whole-life carbon, cost, time and operational performance; document approval rationale.
KPI: % of projects comparing retain, refurbish and new-build options; structural and fit-out mass retained (%); embodied tCO2e and capex avoided; closure or programme days avoided
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Experiential Leisure; Contract Caterers only where delegated asset/capital control is documented
Sector_Not_Included: Exclude sites where the operator does not control the relevant asset, utility, specification or capital decision.

Initiative_Name: Require component reuse and material recovery in building and fit-out projects
Description: Set project requirements for retention, reuse, refurbishment, salvage and high-value recovery of building and fit-out components.
Why_Benefit: Frequent hospitality fit-outs generate furniture, flooring, partitions, equipment and finishes with remaining value. Component reuse reduces replacement purchasing and disposal, can shorten lead times and supports a visible circular-economy story for customers and clients.
How_Text: Pre-demolition/strip-out audit; identify reusable components; set reuse/recovery targets; allocate storage and warranties; procure take-back; evidence final destinations and avoided products.
KPI: % of components retained or reused by mass and value; tonnes sent to reuse, recycling and disposal; replacement purchasing avoided (£); tCO2e avoided
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Projects with no controlled strip-out, fit-out or material scope.
Source_Old_Initiative: Adopt reuse and recycling practices in buildings and fitouts

Initiative_Name: Specify lower-carbon and responsibly sourced construction materials
Description: Use EPD/LCA and responsible-sourcing criteria to select functionally equivalent materials with lower embodied carbon and acceptable technical performance.
Why_Benefit: Hospitality estates purchase similar materials repeatedly across new sites and refurbishments, so specification choices scale quickly. Lower-carbon and responsibly sourced materials reduce embodied emissions and supply-chain or reputation risk without changing the customer service delivered.
How_Text: Identify carbon hotspots; define functional/specification requirements; establish baseline EPD; request alternatives; compare matched units/modules; approve and verify installed quantities.
KPI: Embodied carbon per functional unit for priority materials (kgCO2e); reduction versus baseline specification (%); % of priority material spend responsibly sourced; installed quantity with verified evidence (%)
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Use sustainable and locally-sourced materials in construction and maintenance

Initiative_Name: Specify durability, repairability, modularity and supplier take-back for capital equipment
Description: Use procurement requirements that extend equipment life, enable component repair and replacement, and create a documented end-of-use route.
Why_Benefit: Kitchen, refrigeration and service equipment operates intensively and failures can immediately affect trading. Durability, repairability and take-back requirements reduce downtime, replacement capex, waste and lifetime cost while improving parts and service availability.
How_Text: Prioritise equipment categories; set service-life/spares/repair/take-back requirements; score tenders; record warranty and parts availability; track failures, repairs and final route.
KPI: % of priority tenders meeting durability, repairability, modularity and take-back criteria; median expected service life; repair-versus-replace rate; % of end-of-use equipment returned through an approved route
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Consumables and low-value purchases outside the capital-equipment policy.

Initiative_Name: Design buildings and fit-outs for adaptability, disassembly and material recovery
Description: Design layouts, modules and reversible connections so future changes can occur with less demolition and components can be recovered intact.
Why_Benefit: Hospitality layouts and brand formats change frequently. Adaptable and demountable fit-outs allow future reconfiguration with less closure time, capex and waste, while preserving the recoverable value of partitions, finishes and components.
How_Text: Define likely change scenarios; standardise modules; prefer reversible connections; document disassembly sequence and material passport; protect access for maintenance and removal.
KPI: % of projects with an approved adaptability and disassembly plan; % of fit-out mass or value using reversible connections; recoverable component mass and value; reconfiguration waste avoided
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Experiential Leisure; Contract Caterers only where delegated asset/capital control is documented
Sector_Not_Included: Exclude sites where the operator does not control the relevant asset, utility, specification or capital decision.

Initiative_Name: Commission new buildings and major refurbishments against designed operational performance
Description: Test systems at handover and through seasonal operation, train operators and verify that controls and energy performance match design intent.
Why_Benefit: Complex building systems often consume more energy or deliver poorer comfort than the design intended. Commissioning identifies defects before they become routine, closes the design-to-operation gap and protects investment, guest comfort and operator training.
How_Text: Define commissioning plan at design; witness installation/testing; validate controls and metering; train operators; complete seasonal reviews; compare 12-month energy with target and rectify defects.
KPI: % of projects completing handover and seasonal commissioning; defects closed within the agreed period (%); 12-month design-to-operation energy gap (%); comfort or service-performance exceptions
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Experiential Leisure; Contract Caterers only where delegated asset/capital control is documented
Sector_Not_Included: Exclude sites where the operator does not control the relevant asset, utility, specification or capital decision.

Initiative_Name: Apply verified energy-efficiency criteria when replacing kitchen equipment
Description: Require replacement cooking, warewashing, refrigeration and food-service equipment to meet defined, independently verifiable energy-performance criteria.
Why_Benefit: Commercial kitchen equipment has high energy demand and remains in service for many years. Verified efficiency criteria lock lower running costs into normal replacement cycles across cooking, warewashing, refrigeration and food service without requiring a separate retrofit programme.
How_Text: Identify replacement cycle and high-load categories; set test-standard/ETL criteria; compare lifetime energy and service; procure; record model; verify representative site consumption.
KPI: % of eligible replacement spend meeting ETL or equivalent verified criteria; lifetime energy cost versus baseline (£); annual kWh and tCO2e saved; % of purchased models recorded with evidence
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers
Sector_Not_Included: Sites without commercial kitchen equipment or procurement authority.
Source_Old_Initiative: Replace old kitchen equipment with energy efficient alternatives

Initiative_Name: Assess the feasibility of hydrogen-ready kitchen equipment
Description: Monitor hydrogen-ready commercial-kitchen technology and assess it only where a credible fuel supply, infrastructure route, safety case and operational need exist. Do not treat the assessment as a commitment to purchase or install equipment.
Why_Benefit: Hydrogen supply, infrastructure, equipment availability and whole-system efficiency remain uncertain for commercial kitchens. A structured feasibility assessment prevents stranded investment and compares the option fairly with efficient electric alternatives before capital is committed.
How_Text: Define use case; confirm supply/infrastructure horizon; assess safety, ventilation and training; compare whole-system efficiency/carbon/cost; record decision trigger and review date.
KPI: % of scheduled feasibility reviews completed; projected whole-system kWh, £ and tCO2e versus an efficient electric baseline; infrastructure and safety readiness status; next decision-trigger date
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels and Contract Caterers with relevant gas cooking loads
Sector_Not_Included: Sites without a credible hydrogen supply, safety case, infrastructure route or equipment need.
Source_Old_Initiative: Explore installation of hydrogen-ready kitchen equipment

Initiative_Name: Apply environmental-performance criteria when selecting leased sites
Description: Assess building energy, EPC, utility/meter access, equipment control, renewable procurement and improvement rights before selecting a leased location.
Why_Benefit: A lease decision can lock an operator into poor energy performance, limited metering and weak improvement rights for years. Screening sites before commitment exposes hidden operating and upgrade costs and avoids locations where the operator cannot control material impacts.
How_Text: Set minimum criteria; request bills/EPC/meter and plant data; assess control boundary; estimate normalised energy; price required improvements; include outcome in site approval.
KPI: % of candidate leases assessed before commitment; % meeting the minimum energy, EPC, metering and control standard; forecast energy cost and remedial capex per site; approved exceptions (%)
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Owned freehold acquisitions assessed under the capital-project process.
Source_Old_Initiative: Lease locations in low impact buildings.

Initiative_Name: Apply energy and carbon criteria to lease renewals and franchise onboarding
Description: Use defined performance thresholds and improvement-plan requirements when renewing leases or onboarding franchise locations.
Why_Benefit: Lease renewal and franchise onboarding are rare points of commercial leverage. Applying energy and carbon criteria before signature prevents long-term lock-in and secures data, standards or funded improvement actions while terms can still be negotiated.
How_Text: Set threshold and evidence list; review historic energy and control; identify gaps; agree funded improvement plan and timeline; make approval conditional; track completion.
KPI: % of renewal and onboarding decisions meeting the standard or carrying a funded improvement plan; % of agreed actions delivered by the due date; post-action kWh and tCO2e improvement
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Owned sites and existing franchise operations outside a renewal/onboarding event.

Initiative_Name: Include green performance, data and cooperation clauses in leases and franchise agreements
Description: Embed responsibilities for performance, data access, metering, cooperation, improvement works and evidence in the governing agreement.
Why_Benefit: Split incentives and unclear responsibilities commonly prevent landlords, tenants and franchise partners from acting. Green clauses make data sharing, access, metering, renewable procurement and cost cooperation enforceable, turning viable projects into deliverable actions.
How_Text: Map operational responsibilities; select BBP-aligned clause strength; adapt to asset and commercial terms; secure legal approval; store obligations; monitor compliance and renewal triggers.
KPI: % of agreements containing approved green clauses; % of required energy datasets received on time; clause compliance rate; improvement actions delivered under the clauses
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Owned sites with no lease/franchise agreement.

Initiative_Name: Collect and quality-check energy and emissions data from leased, tenanted and franchised sites
Description: Establish recurring collection, validation, estimation rules and reporting for energy and emissions across leased and franchised sites.
Why_Benefit: Leased, tenanted and franchised estates often lack complete and comparable energy data. Reliable site data identifies high-cost outliers and billing errors, supports credible disclosures and directs operational support and investment to the locations with the greatest opportunity.
How_Text: Define boundary and fields; secure data rights; automate supplier/meter feeds where possible; validate completeness/outliers; document estimates; report trend by control type.
KPI: % of sites submitting complete data on time; % of consumption from primary meter or supplier data; estimated-data share; data-quality exceptions unresolved after 30 days
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Sites outside the agreed organisational/reporting boundary.

Initiative_Name: Secure rights and approval routes for environmental improvements in leased sites
Description: Agree alterations, access, reinstatement, metering and plant-control rights so qualifying tenant or landlord improvements can be implemented.
Why_Benefit: Cost-effective improvements can remain blocked by consent, access, reinstatement or plant-control restrictions. Securing clear approval routes reduces project delays and wasted feasibility work and allows operators to deliver savings during practical maintenance or refurbishment windows.
How_Text: Identify blocked measures; review lease and landlord process; propose rights/consent protocol; agree evidence, access and reinstatement; record approval route and responsible contacts.
KPI: % of priority leases with required alteration, access, metering and plant-control rights; median approval time; % of consent requests approved; blocked projects released
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Owned sites and leases where all relevant rights already exist.

Initiative_Name: Enable renewable electricity procurement under lease and franchise arrangements
Description: Establish landlord, tenant or franchisor routes for renewable electricity where responsibility, metering, evidence and contractual rights permit.
Why_Benefit: Electric kitchens, refrigeration and guest facilities make purchased electricity a material source of cost and emissions. An approved procurement route lets leased and franchised sites reduce market-based Scope 2 emissions without owning the building assets.
How_Text: Map procurement responsibility; define quality criteria; review existing supply contract; select tariff/PPA/landlord route; secure evidence; track renewable share and renewal date.
KPI: % of eligible leased or franchised electricity under an approved renewable procurement route; renewable MWh and share of electricity (%); market-based Scope 2 tCO2e reduced; contracts or evidence expiring within 12 months
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Sites where electricity procurement is outside operator influence and no cooperation route exists.

Initiative_Name: Agree landlord-tenant decarbonisation plans with actions, funding and accountability
Description: Agree a site-level improvement plan that allocates actions, access, funding, cost sharing, data and review responsibilities between landlord and occupier.
Why_Benefit: Shared buildings create split responsibilities in which neither landlord nor occupier can deliver the full opportunity alone. A funded joint plan aligns maintenance, capex, access and lease timing, converting engagement into accountable actions and whole-building savings.
How_Text: Build shared baseline; separate owner/occupier loads; prioritise measures; assign owner/funding/timeline; agree data and review forum; track implementation and verified results.
KPI: % of priority leased sites with a signed, funded decarbonisation plan; % of actions delivered on time; owner and occupier kWh, £ and tCO2e saved; overdue actions by responsible party
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Sector_Not_Included: Owned sites or leases with no shared building/utility responsibility.
Source_Old_Initiative: Engage with landlord to reduce emissions from leased facilities

Initiative_Name: Set and monitor energy-performance standards for franchisees
Description: Define minimum operating, equipment, data and improvement standards for existing franchisees and monitor performance with proportionate escalation.
Why_Benefit: Franchise estates can have a large aggregate footprint but dispersed operational control. Minimum standards, normalised benchmarking and corrective plans scale proven practices, protect brand consistency and help franchisees reduce energy bills and equipment risk.
How_Text: Segment franchise archetypes; define minimum standards and evidence; provide tools/training; collect normalised data; benchmark peers; require corrective plan; recognise and escalate performance.
KPI: % of franchise sites meeting the minimum standard; normalised energy intensity (kWh/site, m² or cover) versus peer median; annual £ and tCO2e improvement; corrective plans closed by the due date
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels and Experiential Leisure with franchise models
Sector_Not_Included: Contract Caterers and organisations without franchise operations.

Initiative_Name: Complete an Energy Health Check
Description: A structured audit of energy consumption across a site or estate that reviews energy usage, reduction and efficiency options, based on smart meter data.
Why_Benefit: Establish where energy is actually used to understand what the potential is to support improvements in energy efficinies through quick wins and behaviour change initaitves. The critical caveat is that an audit identifies savings but does not deliver them.
How_Text:
1. Scope and qualify — confirm whether the group is ESOS-obligated, identify the assets and activities making up at least 95% of total energy consumption and appoint a registered Lead Assessor.
2. Collect verifiable data — gather 12 consecutive months of energy data across buildings, transport and processes from invoices, half-hourly data and meter reads, converted to a common unit.
3. Audit a representative sample — audit sites spanning the ages, sizes and trading formats in the estate, costing every opportunity for capex, annual kWh and £ saving, payback and tCO2e.
4. Convert the report into an action plan — rank measures by payback, scale sample findings to the full estate and feed approved measures into the capital plan with named owners and dates.
KPI: % of sites that have completed an Energy Health Check
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Complete an Energy Health Check, and identify opportunites for energy savings through behavioural change campaigns

Initiative_Name: Install battery storage (BESS)
Description: Installing a behind-the-meter battery energy storage system (BESS) that charges when electricity is cheap or when on-site generation is in surplus, and discharges at times of peak price or peak site demand.
Why_Benefit: Lets a site use more of its own solar generation instead of exporting it, shaves peak demand charges, and provides resilience during outages so trading can continue. It also opens a grid-services revenue stream. The business case is tariff-driven rather than technology-driven: it only works where the price spread between charging and discharging periods exceeds the levelised cost of storage, so evening-weighted loads (pubs, restaurants, hotels) suit it far better than daytime-flat loads.
How_Text:
1. Screen the estate — shortlist sites with a pronounced evening demand peak, existing or planned rooftop solar, physical space and available DNO capacity, prioritising sites with high agreed-capacity charges.
2. Size against half-hourly data — model site load against solar generation to size kWh and kW for peak shaving, solar time-shifting and tariff arbitrage, and confirm the accessible revenue stack.
3. Fund and consent — decide between owned capex and third-party financed structures, and obtain the DNO connection agreement, planning consent and fire-safety and insurer sign-off.
4. Commission and verify — automate charge and discharge through an energy management system, then measure peak kW reduction, self-consumption uplift and any grid-service revenue.
KPI: Cumulative battery storage (BESS) capacity installed (kWh)
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure

Initiative_Name: Upgrade to LED lighting with optimised design and controls
Description: Replacing existing lamps and fittings with LED equivalents, designed to the lighting levels the space actually needs and paired with controls such as occupancy sensing, daylight harvesting and dimming, rather than a like-for-like lamp swap.
Why_Benefit: Lighting can account for up to half the electricity bill in a hospitality site, and LED retrofits are among the shortest-payback measures available - typically 1-3 years on energy alone. The saving is twofold: LEDs draw 50-75% less power than fluorescent, and they last four to five times as long, so relamping and access costs fall alongside energy. Adding controls rather than just changing lamps takes the total saving from around 50-75% to 70-80%.
How_Text:
1. Audit the lighting stock by trading format — inventory fittings by type, wattage and annual run hours and record lux levels, separating long-run-hour back-of-house and external areas from customer-facing space.
2. Design the scheme rather than swap lamps — specify fitting layout, output, colour temperature and controls, then pilot one site per format and sign the design off with operations.
3. Bundle into the capital cycle — procure at estate scale and align installation with planned refurbishments, sequencing by run hours so the longest-running areas go first.
4. Verify and report — compare half-hourly consumption before and after at pilot sites to set a per-format saving factor, and track avoided relamping and maintenance cost alongside energy.
KPI: % of lighting upgraded to LED with optimised design and controls
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Switch to LED lights

Initiative_Name: Install heat/energy recovery ventilation units
Description: Installing ventilation systems that recover heat from outgoing air and transfer it to incoming fresh air, reducing heating or cooling demand.
Why_Benefit: Ventilation is a large and continuous heat loss in hospitality buildings: warm air is extracted from kitchens, bedrooms and function spaces and replaced with cold outside air that must then be heated. Recovering that heat cuts heating demand directly, and is one of the few measures that works on a fully electrified building where there is no gas to switch. Payback is driven almost entirely by run hours and by which fuel the recovered heat displaces, so it should never be quoted as a single estate-wide figure.
How_Text:
1. Locate the waste heat — take extract points by temperature and run hours from the Energy Health Check output, covering kitchen canopies, cellar cooling condensers, hotel corridors and bathrooms, and function-room air handling.
2. Select the recovery route per application — air-to-air exchangers on general ventilation, run-around coils where extract air is contaminated and wastewater recovery on kitchen drains, matching recovered heat to a simultaneous demand.
3. Pilot with measurement — install at one site per format with temperature and flow monitoring and run it across a full heating season before committing to rollout.
4. Roll out at the refurbishment cycle — retrofit when ventilation plant is being replaced or a kitchen refitted, and record recovered kWh per site from the pilot monitoring.
KPI: % of sites with heat/energy recovery ventilation installed
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Install Heat Recovery Ventilation Units

Initiative_Name: Deploy gas boiler additives
Description: Dosing a wet (hydronic) central heating system with a chemical additive intended to improve heat transfer from radiators, so the boiler burns less gas to hold the same internal temperature. Dosed like a corrosion inhibitor, typically at the same time as a powerflush.
Why_Benefit: Heating is the largest single gas load in a hospitality estate - Fuller's discloses that heating accounts for over 50% of the gas used across its sites - so a small percentage gain applies to a large base. Dosing needs no capital works, no system downtime and takes 10-15 minutes per system, making it one of the few gas measures deployable across a whole estate inside a single heating season. The critical caveat is that the additive is almost always dosed alongside a powerflush, and the powerflush delivers a substantial share of the saving on its own.
How_Text:
1. Screen which boilers are eligible — additives work in closed-loop wet heating systems, so exclude sites already scheduled to come off gas and confirm boiler and inhibitor compatibility with the supplier in writing.
2. Establish a normalised baseline — collect at least one full heating season of gas consumption per site and normalise it to heating degree days, or a mild winter will manufacture a saving that does not exist.
3. Run a controlled pilot — dose a sample of sites and leave comparable sites undosed over the same period, changing nothing else, then compare degree-day-normalised consumption between the two groups.
4. Decide, then roll out or stop — extend only if the pilot shows a saving exceeding measurement uncertainty, then track treated boilers alongside normalised gas consumption and re-dose at the supplier's interval.
KPI: % of gas boilers treated with additives
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Use gas boiler additives

Initiative_Name: Install air or ground source heat pumps
Description: Replacing gas or LPG boilers with air source or ground source heat pumps, which move heat from outside air or the ground into the building rather than burning fuel to create it. In hospitality this is normally done at boiler end of life and paired with kitchen and hot-water electrification, since a heat pump alone does not take a site off gas.
Why_Benefit: Gas and LPG equipment is the dominant source of direct emissions in a hospitality estate - Whitbread discloses that over 70% of its Scope 1 emissions come from it - so nothing else removes Scope 1 at this scale. A heat pump delivers three or more units of heat per unit of electricity, so it also converts the estate's remaining fossil load into something that decarbonises automatically as the grid does. The counter-argument is running cost: UK non-domestic electricity costs roughly 4.7 times gas per kWh, so the operating case depends entirely on achieved efficiency and contracted rates.
How_Text:
1. Assess heat demand and fabric first — establish site heat loss, existing emitter sizing and hot water demand before selecting capacity, since heat pumps deliver at lower flow temperatures than gas boilers.
2. Choose the technology per site — air source for most retrofits, ground source only where land and capital justify it, and confirm electrical supply capacity and DNO headroom early.
3. Design the whole electrification package — cover space heating, hot water and kitchen equipment together, retaining buffer vessels, storage or a secondary heat source for peak-demand days.
4. Bundle into the capital cycle and verify — install alongside planned refurbishment so each site is disrupted once, then measure delivered heat against electricity consumed to evidence the achieved coefficient of performance.
KPI: % of sites with gas heating replaced by air or ground source heat pumps (report installed thermal capacity in kW and achieved seasonal COP per site)
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Install air source or ground source heat pumps

Initiative_Name: Utilise cellar cooling across estates
Description: Reducing the energy used to keep a pub cellar and its dispense equipment at serving temperature, through controls that cycle the chiller, free (ambient) cooling, heat recovery from the refrigeration circuit, and replacement of outdated plant. Applies to pubs, bars and breweries only.
Why_Benefit: Cellar equipment runs continuously, all day and every day, which makes it one of the largest and most predictable electricity loads in a pub and the one energy measure that is unique to the sector. The measures are sequenced cheapest-first - controls before plant replacement - so the initiative can start without capital. It also carries a commercial benefit that usually exceeds the energy saving: stable cellar temperature protects drinks quality and cuts beer waste.
How_Text:
1. Survey the cellar as a chilled box — record volume, insulation, door seals and every heat source inside the cooled space, including remote coolers, ice machines and lighting, plus the chiller's age and sizing.
2. Do the no- and low-cost measures first — relocate heat-generating equipment out of the cooled space, fix seals, fit door alarms and correct over-cooling, which often reduces the cooling capacity needed.
3. Add controls and free cooling — fit smart controls that cycle the chiller against measured cellar temperature, and consider an ambient cooler that uses outside air in colder conditions.
4. Sub-meter, then replace the plant last — measure cellar kWh before and after so savings can be evidenced, and replace the cooling unit only once heat gains are reduced so the new unit can be smaller.
KPI: % of sites with cellar cooling installed
Sector_Included: Pubs/Bars/Breweries
Sector_Not_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Utilise Cellar Cooling

Initiative_Name: Replace gas-fired heating and catering equipment with electric alternatives
Description: Replacing gas- and LPG-fired catering equipment, space heating and hot water plant with electric alternatives - induction and electric cooking, electric or heat pump water heating - with the end state being a site that has no gas or LPG connection at all.
Why_Benefit: This is the only measure that removes Scope 1 combustion emissions outright rather than reducing them, and unlike certificate-based measures it produces a physical change that cannot be questioned on additionality grounds. It also removes exposure to future gas price and gas policy risk, and improves kitchen working conditions through lower ambient heat and better indoor air quality. The honest counter-argument is operating cost: UK non-domestic electricity costs roughly 4.7 times gas per kWh, and direct electric catering equipment has no coefficient of performance to offset that, so this initiative is bought for Scope 1 abatement and regulatory resilience, not for energy cost savings.
How_Text:
1. Inventory gas assets and define the end state — list every gas appliance and adopt an auditable definition of 'off gas' covering water heating, space heating and cooking, noting a site is only off gas once the meter is removed.
2. Treat kitchens as the critical path — run menu trials, chef training and equipment selection before rollout, expecting kitchens to electrify well ahead of full site de-gassing.
3. Confirm electrical capacity before committing — check supply capacity and DNO headroom per site, as a supply upgrade is often the largest single cost and the longest lead item.
4. Bundle with planned works, then remove the connection — electrify during refurbishment on REGO-backed supply, then disconnect and remove the gas meter to end standing charges and make the change auditable.
KPI: % of gas-fired heating and catering units replaced with electric alternatives
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Transition from gas to electricity

Initiative_Name: Invest in energy-efficiency and renewables infrastructure
Description: Committing and tracking a defined level of investment in energy-efficiency and renewable-generation assets across the estate, whether funded from the operator's own capital or through third-party finance such as a power purchase agreement.
Why_Benefit: Planned investment is the leading indicator for every other energy measure: without a committed budget, an audit produces a list that is never delivered. Tracking it also makes the transition plan credible to investors and lenders, who increasingly test whether stated targets are backed by capital allocation. The measurement caveat matters as much as the investment: a capital-only metric will score a fully third-party-financed programme at zero, which is exactly the wrong signal.
How_Text:
1. Build the pipeline from evidence — use the Energy Health Check output to assemble a costed list of measures, each with capex, annual saving, payback and tCO2e.
2. Rank and allocate across the portfolio — split spend between quick-payback efficiency measures, structural decarbonisation with long payback, and generation, testing contested measures before funding.
3. Decide the funding route per measure — owned capital, third-party financed PPAs, leasing or supplier finance, tested against cost of capital and contract tenure.
4. Align to the works cycle, then disclose — tie measures to refurbishment, plant end-of-life and lease events, report spend against the KPI, and track delivered kWh, £ and tCO2e against plan.
KPI: Planned capital investment in energy efficiency and renewables over next 12 months (£)
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure

Initiative_Name: Upgrade building-fabric thermal performance (insulation, glazing, draught-proofing)
Description: Improving the thermal performance of the building envelope - roof, wall and floor insulation, glazing, and draught-proofing - so less heat is lost through the fabric and the building needs less energy to hold a comfortable temperature.
Why_Benefit: Fabric improvement lowers heating demand year-round and lasts the life of the building, so it does not decay the way controls settings and behavioural measures do. It is also the enabling investment for electrification: a building with reduced heat loss needs smaller heat pump plant, can run at lower flow temperatures where efficiency is higher, and may avoid an expensive electrical supply upgrade altogether. The avoided cost of that larger supply upgrade can exceed the energy saving itself, which is why fabric usually loses on a standalone payback test but wins when appraised as an enabler.
How_Text:
1. Segment the estate by fabric archetype — group buildings by construction type, age and heritage status, and establish current U-values, glazing type and airtightness per archetype.
2. Specify a conservation-compatible package per archetype — where external wall insulation is not permitted, use roof and loft insulation, secondary or slim-profile glazing, draught-proofing and floor insulation, tackling airtightness first.
3. Pair fabric with ventilation, then resize plant — specify MVHR or equivalent alongside improved airtightness, then size heating plant to the reduced load.
4. Bundle into refurbishment and verify — tie disruptive works to planned refurbishment cycles, verify on degree-day-corrected heating consumption, and report by archetype.
KPI: % of sites that have completed building-fabric thermal upgrades
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Improve building insulation

Initiative_Name: Install smart sub-metering and a building management system (BMS)
Description: Installing half-hourly smart sub-metering and an actively managed building management system, so consumption is visible by site and by load, and HVAC, lighting and refrigeration are controlled automatically rather than manually.
Why_Benefit: Metering is the measurement basis for every other energy measure: without a half-hourly baseline, savings claimed anywhere else are estimates rather than evidence, and no supplier guarantee can be tested. It also surfaces waste that no site visit would catch - plant left running overnight, simultaneous heating and cooling, refrigeration faults before stock is lost. The cheapest wins come from data and controls the operator already owns, which is why this is usually the first initiative to fund and the least capital-intensive to start.
How_Text:
1. Harvest the data you already own — request half-hourly data from suppliers for every site with an advanced meter, then produce a gap list of sites needing meter retrofit.
2. Design a proportionate sub-metering strategy — decide per site format what to meter separately, covering cellar cooling, kitchen, HVAC, lighting, hot water and EV charging, by significant load rather than every item of plant.
3. Profile and hunt anomalies at estate level — build a typical half-hourly profile per site format and flag deviations: plant running overnight, heating and cooling fighting, equipment left on when closed.
4. Re-tune the existing BMS, then automate and assign ownership — audit setpoints, schedules and dead bands before buying hardware, then set a weekly exception review so a named person closes out anomalies.
KPI: % of sites with half-hourly smart sub-metering and an active BMS
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Install smart meters

Initiative_Name: Install on-site solar PV
Description: Installing solar photovoltaic panels on site roofs or land so that electricity is generated where it is consumed, either funded from the operator's own capital or through a third-party financed power purchase agreement.
Why_Benefit: On-site generation displaces grid-purchased electricity physically rather than contractually, so unlike a green tariff it cannot be challenged on additionality and it genuinely reduces the volume of electricity bought. That is the decisive commercial point: Mitchells & Butlers' Property Director has stated publicly that buying 100% renewable electricity made a significant impact on emissions but did not protect the business from price increases - on-site generation does, because a self-consumed unit is never purchased. Where the installation is third-party financed the price protection extends across the contract life at no capital cost.
How_Text:
1. Screen roofs for viability — filter on tenure first, freehold or long leasehold only, then orientation, pitch, roof age and condition, structural load capacity, shading and available area.
2. Size for self-consumption, not roof area — model half-hourly demand against generation and size the array to what the site consumes in daylight, since exported units earn far less than imported units cost; expect roughly 15-20% of a pub's annual demand.
3. Choose the funding route per site tenure — owned capital retains the asset and generation margin; a third-party financed PPA removes the capital constraint but locks in a contract that may outlast tenure.
4. Deliver as a repeatable production line and verify — apply for DNO connection early, standardise designs per roof archetype and batch sites geographically, then meter generation against forecast.
KPI: On-site solar PV capacity installed (kWp) and % of annual electricity demand met by on-site generation
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Install solar panels

Initiative_Name: Install voltage optimisation equipment
Description: Installing equipment that regulates the incoming mains voltage down to a level closer to what site equipment actually requires. UK supply averages around 242V while equipment is rated 207-253V and is generally most efficient near 220V, so the intent is to cut consumption without any change to how the site operates.
Why_Benefit: The attraction is that it needs no behavioural change, no operational disruption and no ongoing management once fitted. The honest position, however, is that this is the one contested technology in this set: savings arise only on voltage-dependent loads, the independent evidence is far weaker than supplier claims, and the saving decays as equipment is replaced with voltage-independent alternatives. Treat it as pilot-gated rather than proven, and size expectations from the lower bound.
How_Text:
1. Measure incoming voltage before considering equipment — log actual supply voltage over at least a week at candidate sites and screen out any already supplied near 220-230V.
2. Profile the load, not just the voltage — separate voltage-dependent consumption such as older motors and discharge lighting from voltage-independent loads such as VSDs, inverter plant and LED drivers.
3. Pilot with independent measurement and verification — install at two or three representative sites, verify to IPMVP against control sites over the same period, and require a savings guarantee.
4. Sequence after other upgrades and re-verify — install only once LED and plant upgrades are decided, since those remove the loads that create the saving; re-measure annually.
KPI: % of sites fitted with voltage optimisation and average % reduction in electricity consumption
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Install voltage optimisation

Initiative_Name: Procure renewable electricity via PPAs or green tariffs
Description: Contracting electricity supply through a long-term power purchase agreement with a named generator, or through a REGO-backed green tariff from a supplier. This measures the procurement decision - the share of demand secured on renewable contractual terms - rather than the electricity actually consumed.
Why_Benefit: A power purchase agreement fixes price and volume for the contract life, so it is a genuine hedge against wholesale volatility as well as a decarbonisation route, and where it funds new-build generation it delivers real additionality. A REGO-backed tariff does neither: it decarbonises reported emissions but leaves the buyer fully exposed to price. That distinction is the whole point of this initiative - the two routes are frequently presented as interchangeable and are not.
How_Text:
1. Map the supply portfolio and contract calendar — list every meter with supplier, contract end date, annual volume and REGO status, then group sites into tranches by renewal date, since expiry dates dictate the achievable timeline.
2. Match a route to each tranche — a REGO-backed tariff for immediate estate-wide coverage, an on-site behind-the-meter PPA for sites with viable roofs, and an off-site or aggregated corporate PPA where volume and credit standing allow.
3. Consider an aggregated PPA across members — operators individually lacking the volume and credit profile for a wholesale agreement can participate collectively under a larger buyer.
4. Tender on certainty and additionality, then evidence it — score bids on contracted price and term, REGO retirement evidence and the age and location of the generating asset, then disclose the split between genuine PPAs and certificated tariffs.
KPI: % of electricity procured under long-term PPAs or REGO-backed green tariffs
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Buy renewable electricity

Initiative_Name: Enroll sites in demand-side response and flexibility schemes
Description: Contracting flexible electrical load - battery storage, EV charging, refrigeration, HVAC - into grid flexibility schemes such as the Capacity Market, so the site is paid to reduce or shift consumption at times of system stress. Usually accessed through an aggregator that bundles many small sites into a tradeable portfolio.
Why_Benefit: This is the only initiative in this set that earns revenue rather than saving cost, and it also reduces peak-related network charges. It rewards flexibility an estate may already have in refrigeration and storage. The honest position is that at current clearing prices the revenue is close to immaterial for a hospitality site, and the response windows collide with peak trading - so it should be treated as a marginal top-up on flexibility investment justified by other value, never as the business case for it.
How_Text:
1. Identify genuinely flexible load — use half-hourly data to find load that can be shifted or briefly interrupted without affecting guests, food safety or trade: refrigeration and cellar cooling, hot water storage, HVAC pre-conditioning, EV charging and battery storage.
2. Check the timing conflict before anything else — flexibility windows typically run roughly 07:00-14:00 and 16:00-22:00 seven days a week, and the evening window is peak trading.
3. Select an aggregator and negotiate the penalty terms deliberately — sites are too small to participate directly, and one missed response can penalise a whole pooled contract.
4. Mandate genuine load shifting, automate with override, then pilot — exclude diesel backup generation in the contract, give managers a documented override for trading-critical moments, and run a full season on a few sites before extending.
KPI: % of sites enrolled in DSR/flexibility schemes and annual load shifted or curtailed (kWh)
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure

Initiative_Name: Run staff energy-engagement programmes
Description: Structured programmes that change how site teams use energy day to day - switch-off routines, energy champions, role-specific training, incentives and visible consumption feedback - rather than changes to plant or building fabric.
Why_Benefit: This is the lowest-cost measure available: the independent evidence puts the required investment at 1-2% of energy spend, and it is almost entirely revenue rather than capital, so it needs no capital approval and can start immediately. It also reaches the losses no equipment upgrade can fix - doors propped open, plant left running after service, controls overridden manually. The honest counterweight is that it is the hardest measure to prove and the easiest to let decay, so the measurement has to be funded as part of the programme rather than added afterwards.
How_Text:
1. Set the measurement basis before launching — identify matched control sites and establish weather-normalised half-hourly baselines.
2. Find the behaviours from the data, not a generic checklist — use half-hourly profiles to identify what staff actually control: plant left running after close, propped cellar doors, extract fans when kitchens are closed, external lighting in daylight.
3. Design for enablement, not awareness — fix physical barriers first with labelled switches, accessible controls and sensible default timeclock settings, so the desired behaviour is the easy one.
4. Build it into how sites are run, fund it and verify — appoint energy champions, add energy checks to shift routines, budget the Carbon Trust benchmark of 1-2% of energy spend, and report measured change against control sites.
KPI: % of sites running an active staff energy-engagement programme
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Train staff on energy saving

Initiative_Name: Optimise heating controls
