Description: Setting heating to deliver heat only where and when it is needed - zoning by area, weather compensation that varies flow temperature with outside conditions, and time and temperature setback outside occupied hours - rather than running to a fixed schedule and a fixed temperature.
Why_Benefit: Even efficient heating plant wastes energy if it heats empty spaces or runs to a fixed timeclock, and control drift is invisible: schedules get overridden for an event and never reset, sensors fail silently, and nobody notices because the building is warm. The commercial attraction is that the highest-value step needs professional time rather than capital, so it can be delivered across a dispersed estate far faster and more cheaply than plant replacement. It also protects trade - correct zoning prevents both cold trading areas and overheated bedrooms, which is why operations teams support this measure when they resist others.
How_Text:
1. Audit what the controls are doing, site by site — record time clocks, setpoints, dead bands, zoning, sensor locations and whether weather compensation and optimum start are enabled, then test against real trading hours on half-hourly data.
2. Correct the free items first — align schedules to trading hours, widen the dead band so heating and cooling stop fighting, enable setback for unoccupied periods and closed days, and switch on weather compensation and optimum start where the plant supports them.
3. Reduce heat demand before adding sophistication — coordinate with planned fabric and ventilation works, as controls on a leaky building deliver less.
4. Add zoning and central control, then prevent drift — control cellars, kitchens, function rooms and trading areas independently on a central platform, with an annual re-commissioning check, out-of-hours alerts and degree-day-corrected verification.
KPI: % of sites with optimised heating controls (zoning, weather compensation, setback)
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Improve heating controls

Initiative_Name: Improve building EPC ratings to B or above
Description: Raising the Energy Performance Certificate rating of sites to band B or above. An EPC is an independently assessed, modelled asset rating of a building's energy performance, carbon-based for non-domestic property, and is the metric used by the Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards regime.
Why_Benefit: EPC band affects whether a property can lawfully be let, what it is worth, and whether lenders will finance it - so the exposure is avoided loss rather than energy saving.  In practical terms, based on household data, upgrading EPC rating from D to B could equate to a 28-63% decrease in energy bills ( an important finding given the volatile geopolitical context. The regulatory case has weakened substantially, however, and the honest position now is that this is primarily a commercial and asset-value initiative. The measures that raise a band - lighting, fabric, metering and controls - cut energy cost and carbon whether or not an EPC threshold ever applies, which is the more durable argument for doing the work.
How_Text:
1. Build an EPC register and establish scope — record rating, expiry, floor area and tenure per site, then segment by regulatory exposure: let buildings over 1,000 sq m, smaller let buildings, owner-occupied sites and Scottish sites under a separate regime.
2. Model the gap and the cost to B — obtain an EPC improvement report per in-scope site, noting that EPC is a modelled asset rating, so prioritise measures that both cut real consumption and move the rating.
3. Sequence upgrades to lease events and refurbishment cycles — align works with lease breaks, renewals and planned refurbishment, since the standard bites when a tenancy is granted, extended or renewed.
4. Deliver through the existing energy programme and track the timetable — treat EPC as the compliance lens over fabric, plant, lighting, controls and generation work already planned, register any valid exemptions, and re-test when secondary legislation is laid.
KPI: % of sites with an EPC rating of B or above
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Improve building energy ratings

Initiative_Name: Connect sites to low-carbon heat networks or solar thermal
Description: Where available, connecting to a low-carbon district heat network or installing solar thermal for hot water displaces gas-fired heating without a full heat-pump retrofit. Tracking the share of sites on low-carbon heat sources captures decarbonisation routes beyond electrification, particularly for sites where heat pumps are impractical.
Why_Benefit: For sites where a heat pump retrofit is impractical - constrained plant space, listed fabric, insufficient electrical capacity - a heat network connection or solar thermal can decarbonise heat without a full electrification programme. The position has also changed from optional to potentially mandatory: heat network zoning in England can require larger non-domestic buildings inside a designated zone to connect. So this initiative now carries a compliance dimension as well as an opportunity, and the first action is to find out which sites are exposed.
How_Text:
1. Screen by location first — map sites against existing and planned heat networks and designated zones, recording the outcome per site so the KPI denominator reflects what is achievable.
2. Establish the heat and hot water profile before choosing a technology — quantify volume, temperature requirement and seasonal pattern, noting heat networks suit year-round demand while solar thermal matches summer.
3. Compare against the alternatives on the same basis — appraise solar thermal against wastewater heat recovery, an air source heat pump for hot water, and solar PV on the same roof, since roof area is finite.
4. Interrogate commercial terms, then meter and verify — scrutinise tariff indexation, contract length, exit provisions, the network's carbon intensity and backup before signing, then meter delivered heat and report the two technologies separately.
KPI: % of sites supplied by a low-carbon heat network or solar thermal hot water
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Connect to low-carbon heating

Initiative_Name: Procure certified green gas or biomethane
Description: Buying certified green gas or biomethane for sites that remain on gas, evidenced by Renewable Gas Guarantees of Origin (RGGOs) that are cancelled against the volume consumed. It changes the carbon intensity reported for gas without any change to equipment or to the gas physically burnt on site.
Why_Benefit: It requires no capital, no site works and no operational change, so it is the only way to reduce the reported carbon of gas that cannot yet be electrified - a bridge for residual demand during the transition. Two things must be said alongside that: it costs far more per tonne than most capital measures, and under current rules an SBTi-validated organisation cannot count it toward its Scope 1 target at all. Use it deliberately for genuinely unavoidable residual gas, not as a substitute for capital investment.
How_Text:
1. Quantify residual gas demand and how long it will persist — total annual gas consumption in MWh by site, with a forecast of how that declines as electrification and fabric works are delivered.
2. Price the premium and choose the route — multiply residual MWh by prevailing certificate prices for an indicative annual cost, then decide between a certified supplier tariff and buying and cancelling certificates directly.
3. Screen certificates on quality, not just price — check the Production Support label, since certificates from subsidised plants carry weaker additionality.
4. Confirm acceptability, then retire and report honestly — establish in writing how your reporting framework treats green gas certificates, obtain the annual Cancellation Statement, and report the certified share alongside absolute residual gas volume.
KPI: % of gas procured as certified green gas or biomethane
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Buy green gas

Initiative_Name: Certify sites to ISO 50001 energy management
Description: Certifying sites to ISO 50001, an independently audited energy management standard requiring energy baselines, defined significant energy uses, performance indicators and management review - and, uniquely among ISO standards, demonstrated improvement in energy performance rather than simply a maintained system.
Why_Benefit: It converts energy management from a series of projects into a governed process that must keep improving to retain certification, which is what stops savings decaying once the initial enthusiasm passes. In a UK context the strongest argument is compliance efficiency rather than energy saving: certification covering an organisation's full energy consumption is an alternative ESOS compliance route, so it can discharge an obligation the member already has instead of paying for parallel audits. It is also increasingly requested in B2B procurement questionnaires, which matters for members selling corporate accommodation and events.
How_Text:
1. Decide the ESOS interaction first — establish whether certification will cover all energy use, satisfying ESOS through this route, or only part, requiring separate audits for the remainder.
2. Define the certification scope deliberately — whole estate, a single format or a defined group of sites, since scope drives cost, audit burden and the achievable coverage metric.
3. Build the measurement foundation — baselines from at least 12 months of monitored consumption, significant energy uses identified (cellar cooling, kitchens, HVAC), and performance indicators normalised for weather and trading activity.
4. Embed into existing routines, certify and sustain — attach policy, roles, internal audit and management review to existing operational meetings rather than parallel governance, then maintain an improvement pipeline through annual surveillance on the three-year cycle.
KPI: % of sites covered by an ISO 50001-certified energy management system
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure

Initiative_Name: Install power factor correction
Description: Installing capacitor banks to correct a site's power factor - the proportion of the electricity drawn that does useful work - and right-sizing the agreed supply capacity, so that reactive power penalties and excess capacity charges are removed from the electricity bill.
Why_Benefit: This is a billing correction rather than an energy saving: it removes charges the site is incurring for drawing reactive power and for capacity it does not use, without any change to operations. It suits hospitality specifically because refrigeration, cellar cooling, lifts and HVAC are inductive motor loads, which are what depress power factor. Unusually for this list, the saving is arithmetically calculable from a member's own bill before anyone is engaged - so the screening step costs nothing and the business case does not depend on a supplier's percentage.
How_Text:
1. Screen from the bills at zero cost — check reactive/kVArh, kVA maximum demand and availability charges (~£1/kVA/month) per half-hourly supply; exclude single-phase sites and those with no such charges.
2. Measure actual power factor — survey a representative period including trading peaks, plus harmonics. Penalties bite below ~0.95 (some 0.90–0.92); record depth and frequency below threshold, not the average.
3. Size correction and capacity together — kVAr for ~0.95 (kVA reduction = kW × (1/existing pf − 1/target pf)), then cut Authorised Supply Capacity to actual demand, often the larger saving, keeping headroom.
4. Specify for harmonics — detuned banks where LED drivers, inverters and VSDs distort; automatic correction suits variable load; parallel install, no shutdown.
5. Demand a site-specific projection from your bills and survey; reject generic percentage quotes.
6. Monitor for drift — capacitors and controls fail silently; alert on reactive and kVA charges monthly, recheck pf annually. Report % sites corrected and measured pf against qualifying sites, not the whole estate.
KPI: % of sites with power factor correction installed and average power factor achieved
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Install power factor correction

Initiative_Name: Build to BREEAM 'Very Good' or above
Description: An independently certified standard for the design and construction of energy- and resource-efficient buildings. Applying it to new builds and major refurbishments, and targeting a rating of 'Very Good' or above, sets low operational energy demand into the design at the point where it is cheapest to influence.
Why_Benefit: Design-stage decisions determine a building's energy demand for its whole life, and they cost almost nothing to influence at inception and a great deal to change later. The evidence for 'Very Good' is unusually favourable: the scheme owner's own cost research puts the capital uplift below 0.25% of construction cost, so this is close to a free commitment provided the target is set at project inception. Certification also carries value and financing benefits, and on some sites it is imposed by planning conditions regardless of policy.
How_Text:
1. Define 'qualifying project' — all new builds, major refurbishments above a stated capital value or floor area, and anything needing planning consent (some authorities mandate it); otherwise denominators differ.
2. Set the target at inception, not design freeze — credits are cheap designed in, costly retrofitted: the same rating costs under 0.25% or several percent purely on timing. Write it into the brief and appointments.
3. Appoint a licensed assessor at concept design — sort credits into free, cheap and expensive; aim above 'Very Good' as credits are lost in build.
4. Budget the evidence effort — capital uplift is minimal at Very Good, but design and contractor evidence time is real; fund it in fees.
5. Earn credits from planned work — fabric, controls, lighting, heat pumps and on-site generation are delivered anyway; check EPC alongside.
6. Hold to completion — contractor obligation with evidence milestones and post-construction certificate; report certified, not targeted.
KPI: % of qualifying new-build and major refurbishment projects achieving BREEAM 'Very Good' or above
Sector_Included: Restaurants, QSRs, Pubs/Bars/Breweries, Hotels, Contract Caterers, Experiential Leisure
Source_Old_Initiative: Build to green building standards

Initiative_Name: Allocate responsibility at Board level
Description: Assign formal oversight and accountability for sustainability and climate-related matters to the Board, ensuring sustainability is integrated into strategic decision-making and organisational governance.
Why_Benefit: Visible Board ownership demonstrates leadership commitment and ensures sustainability is treated as a strategic business issue rather than an operational initiative. Effective Board oversight strengthens accountability, supports better decision-making and helps ensure sufficient resources are allocated to deliver Net Zero objectives.
How_Text: Assign responsibility for sustainability and climate-related matters to a designated Board member, Board committee or equivalent governing body. Clearly define decision-making authority, reporting lines and responsibilities, including oversight of climate-related risks, opportunities, targets and performance. Ensure sustainability is a standing agenda item at Board meetings and is considered when approving business strategy, investment decisions and major organisational changes.

Description: Appoint a named individual with responsibility for leading, coordinating and monitoring sustainability activities across the organisation.
Why_Benefit: Without clear ownership, sustainability initiatives often become fragmented across departments. A dedicated lead improves coordination, maintains momentum, supports consistent decision-making and ensures accountability for delivering sustainability and Net Zero objectives.
How_Text: Appoint a dedicated sustainability lead or assign responsibility to an existing senior employee, depending on organisational size and resources. Clearly define responsibilities, including coordinating cross-functional initiatives, overseeing sustainability data collection, monitoring KPIs, supporting regulatory compliance, managing sustainability reporting and engaging internal and external stakeholders. Ensure regular reporting to senior management and the Board.

A dedicated governance forum improves collaboration, clarifies ownership, resolves implementation challenges and ensures sustainability is consistently embedded into operational and strategic decision-making.
How_Text: Establish a cross-functional Sustainability Committee with representatives from key business functions. Define clear roles, meeting schedules and responsibilities for overseeing sustainability initiatives, reviewing performance, managing risks and supporting delivery of the Net Zero Strategy.

Review KPIs annually to ensure they remain aligned with organisational priorities and long-term sustainability objectives.

KPI: Conduct at least one formal climate/sustainability engagement with key shareholders or investors annually. Track shareholder support for climate-related resolutions, number of substantive climate engagements and actions arising from stakeholder feedback.

Why_Benefit: Regular performance reviews enable organisations to identify issues early, make informed decisions and maintain momentum towards sustainability objectives. Ongoing monitoring also improves accountability and supports continual improvement.

Initiative_Name: Develop a sustainability strategy informed by a double materiality assessment.
Description: Develop a long-term sustainability strategy based on a double materiality assessment, identifying the environmental, social and governance issues that are most significant to both the organisation and its stakeholders.
Why_Benefit: A sustainability strategy provides a clear long-term direction for decision-making, ensuring resources are focused on the issues that matter most. Using a double materiality approach helps organisations balance business resilience with environmental and social responsibility while responding to evolving stakeholder expectations.
How_Text: Conduct a double materiality assessment to evaluate both the financial impacts of sustainability issues on the organisation and the organisation's impacts on people and the environment. Engage internal and external stakeholders, identify material topics, prioritise key sustainability issues and develop a Board-approved sustainability strategy aligned with the organisation's purpose, business objectives and long-term value creation. Initiative_Name: Calculate your baseline GHG footprint.
Description: Develop a complete greenhouse gas inventory across Scope 1, Scope 2 and relevant Scope 3 emissions to establish a baseline for measuring future progress.
Why_Benefit: A robust emissions baseline provides the foundation for setting targets, prioritising emissions reduction opportunities and monitoring progress over time. Without understanding current emissions, organisations cannot develop credible decarbonisation strategies.
How_Text: Define organisational and operational boundaries using the GHG Protocol. Calculate emissions across Scope 1, Scope 2 and relevant Scope 3 categories using recognised emission factors. Identify emissions hotspots, document assumptions and establish annual reporting processes. Improve data quality over time through supplier engagement and increased use of primary data.
KPI: Complete a Scope 1, 2 and relevant Scope 3 GHG inventory covering ≥95% of estimated material emissions, with a documented baseline year and methodology. Update the inventory annually and monitor data quality/completeness.

Identify climate-related business opportunities such as resource efficiency, low-carbon products, renewable energy and circular business models. Integrate findings into enterprise risk management, business strategy, investment decisions and financial planning.

Description: Identify and access external financial support to accelerate decarbonisation projects and reduce implementation costs.
Why_Benefit: External funding can improve project viability, accelerate implementation and reduce the financial burden associated with decarbonisation investments.
How_Text: Monitor available grants, tax incentives, green finance opportunities and sector-specific funding programmes. Assess eligibility, prepare robust business cases and integrate successful funding into the organisation's wider investment programme.
KPI: Review relevant external funding opportunities at least quarterly. Track number/value of applications, success rate, £ external funding secured, % of eligible decarbonisation CAPEX externally funded and emissions reductions enabled by funded projects.

Initiative_Name: Develop a carbon removals strategy and quality criteria.
Description: Define when carbon removals may be used, establish acceptable removal methods and specify the quality criteria that removal projects must meet.
Why_Benefit: A robust carbon removals strategy ensures removals are used responsibly, maintains the credibility of Net Zero claims and reduces the risk of relying on low-quality carbon credits.
How_Text: Quantify expected residual emissions after feasible reductions. Establish a removals policy and quality criteria covering issues such as additionality, durability/permanence, leakage, robust quantification, monitoring and independent verification. Establish governance for procurement and claims and periodically reassess the strategy as standards and technologies develop.
KPI: 100% of removals used for Net Zero neutralisation meet the organisation's documented quality criteria. Track tonnes of residual emissions, tCO₂ permanently removed, removal durability and % of Net Zero progress achieved through direct reductions versus removals.

Initiative_Name: Involve your guests in sustainability initiatives- offer discounts for opting out of daily cleaning of the room-- ask them to give feedback on your activities
Description: Encourage guests to actively participate in sustainability initiatives that reduce the environmental impact of their stay while increasing awareness of the organisation's sustainability commitments.
Why_Benefit: Guest behaviour can have a significant impact on energy use, water consumption, waste generation and laundry requirements within accommodation businesses. Engaging guests helps reduce operational environmental impacts while increasing awareness of sustainability, strengthening customer trust and supporting the organisation's wider sustainability and Net Zero objectives.
How_Text: Develop guest-facing initiatives that encourage more sustainable behaviours throughout their stay. Examples include offering guests the option to opt out of daily housekeeping or towel and linen changes, promoting water and energy conservation, encouraging the use of refillable water stations and sustainable transport options, and communicating the environmental benefits of participation. Where appropriate, provide incentives such as loyalty points, food and beverage vouchers or charitable donations. Regularly collect guest feedback on sustainability initiatives and use insights to improve future programmes.
KPI: Achieve ≥50% participation in eligible towel/linen reuse or reduced-housekeeping programmes, while maintaining guest-satisfaction scores. Track avoided housekeeping services, laundry loads and estimated water/energy savings per occupied room.
Sector_Included: All
Source_Old_Initiative: New Initiaitve

Initiative_Name: Provide sustainability training for your leadership team, operations and functional central support teams.
Description: Training designed to equip senior leaders and operations teams with the knowledge needed to oversee sustainability strategy, climate risks, targets and organisational accountability.
Why_Benefit: Training builds the knowledge and skills needed to deliver the organisation's sustainability strategy. It improves decision-making, strengthens accountability and helps embed sustainability into day-to-day operations and business planning.
How_Text: Develop a structured sustainability training programme tailored to different roles across the organisation. Cover topics such as climate change, Net Zero, carbon emissions, energy efficiency, waste reduction, sustainable procurement, food waste (where applicable), relevant regulations and individual responsibilities. Include sustainability within employee onboarding, leadership development and mandatory refresher training, and monitor participation and training effectiveness.
KPI: ≥90% of relevant employees complete sustainability training annually, with ≥80% achieving the required post-training knowledge score. Include sustainability training in 100% of relevant new-starter onboarding.

Initiative_Name: Offer a sustainable pension to employees (Ideally make it the default choice)
Description: Offer employees workplace pension investment options that incorporate environmental, social and governance (ESG) considerations, ideally making the sustainable option the default fund where appropriate.
Why_Benefit: Sustainable pension options allow employees to align their retirement savings with responsible investment principles while supporting investment in organisations and projects contributing to the transition to a low-carbon economy.
How_Text: Work with pension providers to identify sustainable investment options that align with recognised responsible investment principles. Clearly communicate available options to employees and consider making the sustainable fund the default option where permitted, while maintaining employee choice. Review pension providers and investment options periodically to ensure they continue to meet recognised sustainability standards.
KPI: 100% of employees have access to a sustainable pension option. Where appropriate, establish a sustainable default and track % of employees invested in it. Require annual reporting on financed-emissions intensity and progress against the pension fund's climate targets.
Sector_Included: All

Initiative_Name: Understand employee sustainability expectations and strengthen engagement
Description: Engage employees to understand their sustainability expectations and encourage active participation in delivering the organisation's sustainability objectives.
Why_Benefit: Engaged employees are more likely to support sustainability initiatives, contribute new ideas and adopt more sustainable behaviours. Employee engagement also strengthens organisational culture, improves retention and reinforces the credibility of sustainability commitments.
How_Text: Gather employee feedback through surveys, workshops, engagement sessions and regular communications to understand sustainability priorities and identify opportunities for improvement. Encourage employee participation through Green Teams, sustainability champions, volunteering initiatives, idea-sharing programmes and recognition schemes. Regularly communicate sustainability progress and demonstrate how employee feedback influences organisational decisions.
KPI: Conduct an employee sustainability survey at least annually and achieve ≥60% response rate. Establish employee sustainability representation across relevant functions/sites and track participation in sustainability initiatives. Respond formally to 100% of material themes identified through employee feedback.
Sector_Included: All

Initiative_Name: Embed sustainability into employee roles and responsibilities
Description: Clearly define how sustainability contributes to individual roles and responsibilities, ensuring sustainability becomes part of day-to-day decision-making and performance.
Why_Benefit: Sustainability cannot be delivered by a single team alone. Embedding sustainability into individual roles creates shared ownership, strengthens accountability and ensures sustainability is considered in everyday operational and strategic decisions.
How_Text: Identify how sustainability applies to different functions across the organisation, including operations, procurement, facilities, HR, finance, marketing and leadership. Update job descriptions, objectives and performance expectations where appropriate to reflect sustainability responsibilities. Ensure managers communicate expectations clearly and provide employees with the resources needed to fulfil their responsibilities.
KPI: 100% of roles identified as materially influencing sustainability have documented sustainability responsibilities. Include measurable sustainability objectives in ≥90% of relevant employee/manager performance plans and review progress at least annually.

Initiative_Name: Recognizing and rewarding employees for their contributions to sustainability efforts can boost morale and motivation
Description: Establish formal mechanisms to recognise and, where appropriate, reward employees or teams that contribute to achieving sustainability objectives, implementing environmental improvements or developing innovative sustainability solutions.
Why_Benefit: Recognition reinforces desired behaviours, makes sustainability contributions visible and can strengthen employee motivation and participation. Well-designed rewards can encourage continued pro-environmental behaviour while demonstrating that sustainability performance is valued by the organisation.
How_Text: Define clear eligibility and criteria linked to measurable sustainability outcomes or meaningful behaviours. Use a mix of non-financial recognition—such as awards, internal recognition and development opportunities—and proportionate financial or team incentives where appropriate. Reward both outcomes and the actions that produced them to avoid encouraging gaming of individual metrics. Communicate successful initiatives across the organisation.
KPI: Establish a formal sustainability recognition mechanism and review nominations at least annually or quarterly. Track number of recognised employees/teams, participation rate and environmental outcomes associated with rewarded initiatives. Aim for 100% of sustainability awards to be supported by measurable impact or verified contribution.

Initiative_Name: Develop and maintain a Climate Transition Plan.
Description: Develop and maintain a Climate Transition Plan that outlines how the organisation will achieve its climate and Net Zero commitments through defined actions, governance, investment, timelines and performance monitoring.
Why_Benefit: A Climate Transition Plan provides a structured roadmap for achieving climate commitments and translating strategic ambitions into practical actions. It supports long-term decision-making, improves organisational resilience, strengthens investor and stakeholder confidence and ensures climate considerations are integrated into business planning and investment decisions.
How_Text: Develop the plan in alignment with the organisation's sustainability strategy, GHG baseline and Net Zero targets. Identify material Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions sources and corresponding decarbonisation levers. Define short-, medium- and long-term actions, responsible owners, required investment, implementation timelines and dependencies. Integrate the plan into business planning, financial planning, risk management and governance processes. Establish metrics and interim milestones, disclose progress regularly and update the plan when material changes in regulation, technology, business activity or performance occur.
KPI: Maintain a Board-approved Climate Transition Plan covering 100% of material Scope 1, 2 and relevant Scope 3 emissions. Assign accountable owners and timelines to 100% of priority actions and review progress against quantified interim targets at least annually.
Sector_Included: All
Source_Old_Initiative: New Initiaitve

Initiative_Name: Disclose climate-related information using recognised reporting frameworks (e.g. UK SRS, IFRS S2 and TCFD).
Description: Disclose climate-related governance, strategy, risks, opportunities, metrics and performance using recognised sustainability reporting frameworks to improve transparency and accountability.
Why_Benefit: Transparent climate reporting helps organisations demonstrate accountability, build trust with investors, customers and other stakeholders, and communicate progress towards sustainability objectives. Consistent reporting also supports better decision-making and prepares organisations for evolving reporting requirements.
How_Text: Identify the reporting frameworks most appropriate to the organisation and establish processes for collecting, managing and verifying sustainability data. Report climate-related governance, risks, opportunities, emissions, targets and progress consistently using recognised frameworks. Ensure disclosures are supported by reliable evidence and review reporting processes regularly to improve data quality and meet evolving stakeholder expectations.
KPI: Publish climate-related disclosures annually in accordance with all applicable reporting requirements, covering governance, strategy, risk management and metrics/targets. Aim for 100% disclosure of applicable material requirements, track data completeness and obtain independent assurance over material climate metrics where proportionate and appropriate.
Sector_Included: All

Initiative_Name: Ensure compliance with applicable environmental legislation and reporting requirements (e.g. SECR, ESOS, Simpler Recycling, EPR and the Green Claims Code, where applicable).
Description: Establish a systematic process to identify, monitor and comply with applicable environmental legislation, sustainability reporting obligations and environmental claims guidance relevant to the organisation's activities.
Why_Benefit: Maintaining compliance reduces legal, financial and reputational risks while ensuring the organisation meets evolving regulatory requirements and stakeholder expectations. A proactive compliance process also strengthens governance and supports credible sustainability performance.
How_Text: Identify applicable environmental legislation, reporting obligations and regulatory guidance based on the organisation's size, activities and locations. Assign responsibility for monitoring regulatory developments, implement processes to maintain compliance and regularly review legal obligations. Ensure environmental claims used in marketing and communications are accurate, evidence-based and supported by robust data to minimise greenwashing risks.
KPI: 100% of applicable environmental obligations recorded with a named owner and evidence requirement; 0 overdue corrective actions; compliance status reviewed at least quarterly and after material regulatory changes.

Initiative_Name: Implement an Environmental Management System (e.g. ISO 14001).
Description: Implement an Environmental Management System (EMS) to systematically identify, manage, monitor and continually improve the organisation's environmental performance.
Why_Benefit: An Environmental Management System provides a structured framework for improving environmental performance, strengthening compliance, reducing environmental risks and embedding continuous improvement throughout the organisation. It also supports the delivery of broader sustainability and Net Zero objectives.
How_Text: Establish an Environmental Management System appropriate to the organisation's size and activities. Identify significant environmental aspects and impacts, establish objectives and performance indicators, assign responsibilities, implement documented procedures and regularly monitor performance through audits and management reviews. Where appropriate, pursue ISO 14001 certification to demonstrate alignment with internationally recognised best practice.
KPI: 100% of significant environmental aspects covered by documented controls and objectives; corrective actions closed by their due dates; at least 1 formal management review completed annually.

Initiative_Name: Pursue recognised sustainability certifications and voluntary commitments (e.g. Green Key, Green Tourism, B Corp, Race to Zero or The Climate Pledge)
Description: Pursue recognised sustainability certifications and voluntary commitments that demonstrate environmental leadership, strengthen governance and provide independent recognition of sustainability performance.
Why_Benefit: Recognised certifications and voluntary commitments provide external validation of sustainability performance, strengthen stakeholder confidence and encourage continuous improvement. They can also enhance reputation, improve customer trust and support competitive differentiation within the hospitality sector.
How_Text: Assess which certifications or voluntary commitments are most relevant to the organisation's activities and sustainability objectives. Conduct a gap analysis against certification requirements, implement necessary operational improvements and maintain evidence to demonstrate compliance. Review certification performance regularly and communicate achievements transparently while continuing to drive improvement.
KPI: 100% of priority sites, products or business units assessed against the selected scheme; certification achieved and maintained for the approved scope; 100% of material non-conformities closed by their due dates.

Initiative_Name: Establish a Management Information System to Track Sustainability KPIs Monthly
Description: A system that captures environmental data across key topics and reviews it on a monthly basis, rather than only at annual reporting intervals.
Why_Benefit: Annual reporting is too slow to catch problems early. Monthly tracking lets a business identify variances in time to act, stay accountable to targets and direct management attention toward the initiatives with the greatest commercial and environmental impact.
How_Text: Define a controlled monthly data calendar covering energy, carbon, water, waste, procurement and delivery KPIs. Assign a named owner and reviewer to each metric, automate source-data feeds where practical, investigate material variances and record corrective actions. Use one agreed calculation methodology and retain evidence for audit and annual disclosure.
KPI: 12 monthly performance reviews completed each year; 100% of material KPIs submitted and approved by the monthly close; 100% of material variances assigned to an owner with a due date; 0 unexplained material variances at year-end.
Sector_Included: All

Initiative_Name: Reduce the volume and impact of packaging materials used.
Description: Reduce unnecessary primary, secondary and tertiary packaging while maintaining product protection, food safety and quality. Prioritise eliminating packaging first, followed by reducing material use and selecting lower-impact packaging where packaging remains necessary.
Why_Benefit: Reducing packaging at source lowers material consumption and waste generation and can reduce procurement, transport, storage and waste-management costs. It can also reduce packaging-related Scope 3 emissions and, for obligated UK producers, packaging EPR disposal fees.
How_Text: Establish a baseline of packaging used by material and weight. Review primary, secondary and tertiary packaging to identify unnecessary components and opportunities to reduce weight, dimensions or material use without compromising food safety or product quality. Work with suppliers to trial lighter or simplified formats and prioritise reusable, recyclable or recycled-content alternatives where packaging cannot be eliminated. Track packaging use against the baseline and review specifications regularly.
KPI: Packaging intensity: kg packaging per unit/product/£ revenue. Packaging reduction: tonnes and % reduction in packaging against baseline. Packaging eliminated: number of packaging components/items removed. Financial: £ packaging procurement/EPR cost avoided annually. Carbon: tCO₂e avoided from packaging reductions.
Sector_Included: All
Source_Old_Initiative: Optimise packaging materials - Reduce packaging materials used, and waste generated

Initiative_Name: Collaborate with suppliers to reduce packaging impacts across the supply chain
Description: Work collaboratively with suppliers to reduce the environmental impact of packaging associated with purchased goods, deliveries and customer-facing products, including through packaging elimination, reduction, reuse, recycled content and improved recyclability.
Why_Benefit: A significant proportion of packaging is determined upstream by suppliers rather than by hospitality businesses themselves. Supplier engagement can therefore identify packaging reductions that businesses cannot achieve independently, reducing packaging waste, associated Scope 3 emissions and potentially procurement, logistics, waste-management and EPR-related costs.
How_Text: Identify suppliers responsible for the largest volumes of packaging and engage them to review packaging specifications. Agree opportunities to eliminate unnecessary packaging, reduce material use, increase recycled content and introduce reusable or returnable packaging. Incorporate packaging requirements into procurement specifications and supplier reviews, and track agreed reductions over time.
KPI: Supplier engagement: % of priority suppliers engaged on packaging reduction. Packaging reduction: tonnes and % packaging avoided through supplier initiatives. Reuse: % or number of deliveries using reusable/returnable packaging. Financial: £ annual savings generated through supplier packaging improvements. Carbon: tCO₂e avoided through implemented supplier packaging changes.
Sector_Included: All
Source_Old_Initiative: Engage and work with current suppliers to reduce the impact of packaging

Initiative_Name: Use dispense or refill systems for drinks rather than single-use packaging
Description: Replace individually packaged drinks with dispense, tap, keg or refill systems where feasible to reduce reliance on single-use bottles and cans.
Why_Benefit: Dispense and refill systems can reduce single-use packaging, associated carbon emissions and waste, while also reducing beverage purchasing, transport, storage and waste-management costs. High-volume hospitality operations may achieve particularly strong financial and environmental benefits.
How_Text: Identify high-volume beverages currently purchased in single-use bottles or cans, such as water, soft drinks, beer and wine. Assess suitable alternatives including filtered water systems, post-mix soft drinks, draught beer and wine-on-tap or keg systems. Compare equipment, maintenance and operating costs against current purchasing and waste costs, trial suitable systems and monitor packaging, cost and carbon savings.
KPI: Single-use packaging avoided: number of bottles/cans avoided per year. Packaging reduction: kg/tonnes of packaging avoided. Financial: £ saving per drink and £ annual saving. Carbon: kg/tCO₂e avoided annually. Adoption: % of applicable drinks served through dispense/refill systems.
Sector_Included: All – particularly relevant for hotels, pubs, bars, restaurants, contract caterers and event venues
Source_Old_Initiative: Use dispense options for drinks where possible

Initiative_Name: Undertake life cycle assessment (LCA) of packaging to understand its full environmental impact
Description: Assess the environmental impacts of packaging across its life cycle, including raw material extraction, manufacturing, transport and end-of-life, to identify packaging options with lower overall environmental impacts and avoid shifting impacts between life-cycle stages.
Why_Benefit: Packaging that appears more sustainable based on a single characteristic, such as weight or recyclability, may have greater impacts elsewhere in its life cycle. LCA enables businesses to compare packaging alternatives systematically and identify options that reduce overall environmental impacts while maintaining product protection, food safety and operational performance.
How_Text: Prioritise high-volume or high-impact packaging formats for assessment. Define the scope and functional unit, collect data on packaging materials, manufacturing, transport and end-of-life, and compare alternative packaging options using recognised LCA methodology, software or specialist support. Use the findings alongside cost, food-safety and operational considerations when making packaging decisions.
KPI: Coverage: % of priority packaging formats assessed using LCA. Improvement: % reduction in lifecycle GHG emissions between existing and proposed packaging. Materials: kg of material avoided per packaging unit. Implementation: % of LCA recommendations implemented. Financial: % reduction in packaging costs following LCA-informed redesign.
Sector_Included: All
Source_Old_Initiative: Life cycle analysis (LCA) on packaging

Initiative_Name: Eliminate single-use plastic items from operations
Description: Eliminate avoidable single-use plastic items and packaging from operations and replace them with reusable or refillable alternatives where practical, while maintaining food safety, hygiene, product quality and customer experience.
Why_Benefit: Eliminating single-use plastics reduces material consumption, packaging waste and associated lifecycle emissions. Reusable and refillable alternatives can also reduce recurring purchasing and waste-management costs. In England, certain single-use plastic items are already banned or restricted, including plastic cutlery, drink stirrers and expanded/extruded polystyrene food and drink containers.
How_Text: Audit single-use plastic items across operations and quantify annual usage by item and weight. Prioritise items that can be eliminated completely, followed by those that can be replaced with reusable or refillable systems. For example, replace hotel toiletry miniatures with bulk dispensers, bottled water with refill systems, and disposable serviceware with reusable alternatives. Update procurement specifications, engage suppliers and track reductions against the baseline.
KPI: Plastic eliminated: kg/tonnes of single-use plastic avoided annually. Items eliminated: number of single-use plastic items avoided annually. Reduction: % reduction in single-use plastic against baseline. Financial: £ annual purchasing/waste costs avoided. Carbon: tCO₂e avoided through elimination/reuse.
Sector_Included: All – guest amenities particularly relevant for hotels and other accommodation providers
Source_Old_Initiative: New Initiative

Initiative_Name: Increase recycled content in packaging materials
Description: Increase the proportion of recycled material used in packaging, including plastic, glass, aluminium, paper and cardboard, where food safety, quality and performance requirements allow.
Why_Benefit: Increasing recycled content reduces demand for virgin raw materials and can lower the lifecycle carbon footprint of packaging. For plastic packaging, it can also provide a financial benefit through the UK Plastic Packaging Tax where applicable.
How_Text: Establish the current recycled content of key packaging formats and identify high-volume packaging with low or no recycled content. Work with packaging suppliers to increase recycled content while maintaining food safety, quality and performance. Prioritise high-volume materials and incorporate minimum recycled-content requirements into procurement specifications and supplier reviews.
KPI: Recycled content: % recycled content by packaging material. Virgin material avoided: tonnes/year. Coverage: % of packaging meeting minimum recycled-content requirements. Financial: £ Plastic Packaging Tax avoided where applicable. Carbon: tCO₂e avoided through substitution of virgin material.
Sector_Included: All – particularly relevant for breweries, pubs/bars and businesses using high volumes of packaged products
Source_Old_Initiative: New initiative

Initiative_Name: Evaluate equipment purchases based on full life-cycle cost and environmental impact
Description: Evaluate equipment based on its total cost and environmental impact over its expected lifetime rather than purchase price alone, considering acquisition, energy and water consumption, maintenance, lifespan and end-of-life costs.
Why_Benefit: Equipment with a higher upfront cost may have a lower total cost of ownership and environmental impact if it uses less energy and water, requires less maintenance or lasts longer. Life-cycle costing helps businesses identify the option offering the best overall financial and environmental performance over its useful life.
How_Text: For significant equipment purchases, compare shortlisted options using a standard life-cycle cost assessment. Include purchase and installation costs, expected energy and water consumption, maintenance and repair costs, expected lifespan and end-of-life costs or residual value. Where data are available, compare lifecycle carbon impacts alongside financial costs and incorporate LCC criteria into procurement decisions.
KPI: Coverage: % of significant equipment purchases assessed using LCC. Financial: £ lifetime cost and £ lifetime saving versus alternative equipment. Energy: kWh/year and lifetime kWh saved. Water: m³/year saved where relevant. Carbon: tCO₂e avoided over expected equipment life. Performance: expected equipment lifespan and maintenance cost/year.
Sector_Included: All – particularly relevant for hotels, contract caterers, restaurants and other equipment-intensive operations
Source_Old_Initiative: Consider the full lifecycle costs and impacts of equipment at purchase

Initiative_Name: Shift from equipment ownership to service or leasing models
Description: Use service or leasing models instead of purchasing equipment outright where appropriate, with providers retaining responsibility for maintenance, performance, upgrades and end-of-life recovery or reuse.
Why_Benefit: Service and leasing models can reduce upfront capital requirements and transfer responsibility for equipment maintenance and end-of-life management to the provider. Where contracts incentivise durability, repair and reuse, they can also extend equipment life, reduce material consumption and support more circular asset management.
How_Text: Identify equipment suitable for service or leasing models, such as lighting, coffee machines, laundry equipment, refrigeration and HVAC. Compare the whole-life cost and environmental impact of leasing/service contracts against outright purchase. Prioritise providers offering maintenance, repair, performance guarantees, upgrades and end-of-life take-back, reuse or recycling, and include these requirements in procurement contracts.
KPI: Adoption: % of suitable equipment under service/leasing models. Financial: £ upfront capital avoided and £ annual/lifetime cost versus ownership. Energy: kWh/year saved. Carbon: tCO₂e avoided. Circularity: % of equipment/materials returned for reuse, refurbishment or recycling at end of contract.
Sector_Included: All – particularly relevant for equipment-intensive operations such as hotels, contract caterers and breweries
Source_Old_Initiative: Switch from ownership to service leasing model

Initiative_Name: Prioritise reused, refurbished and responsibly sourced furniture and fittings
Description: Prioritise the reuse, repair and refurbishment of existing furniture and fittings before purchasing new items. Where new products are required, select durable, repairable products made from recycled or responsibly sourced materials.
Why_Benefit: Reusing and refurbishing furniture extends asset life, avoids waste and reduces the need for new materials and manufacturing, lowering embodied carbon. It can also reduce procurement and disposal costs. Where new furniture is necessary, responsible sourcing can reduce environmental impacts and support more sustainable material supply chains.
How_Text: Audit existing furniture and fittings before purchasing new items and identify what can be retained, repaired, refurbished or redistributed. Where additional furniture is required, consider reused or remanufactured products before buying new. For new purchases, prioritise durable and repairable products containing recycled or responsibly sourced materials and request recognised certification where relevant, such as FSC-certified timber. Incorporate reuse, durability, repairability and end-of-life requirements into procurement specifications.
KPI: Reuse: % of furniture requirements met through existing/reused/refurbished assets. Waste: number and tonnes of furniture items diverted from disposal. Financial: £ saved versus equivalent new furniture. Carbon: kg/tCO₂e avoided versus purchasing new. Responsible sourcing: % of new furniture meeting specified sustainability/certification requirements.
Sector_Included: All – particularly relevant for hotels, restaurants, pubs/bars and other businesses undertaking refurbishments or fit-outs
Source_Old_Initiative: Responsibly source furniture and fittings

Initiative_Name: Extend equipment life and manage WEEE through repair, refurbishment, reuse and responsible recycling
Description: Extend the useful life of electrical and electronic equipment through maintenance, repair, refurbishment and redeployment wherever practical. Where equipment can no longer be reused, ensure it is managed through appropriate WEEE recovery and recycling routes.
Why_Benefit: Extending equipment life delays replacement purchases, reduces demand for new equipment and avoids some of the embodied carbon associated with manufacturing new assets. Repair and refurbishment can also reduce procurement costs, while responsible WEEE management keeps reusable components and valuable materials in circulation and supports regulatory compliance.
How_Text: Maintain an asset register and identify equipment suitable for maintenance, repair, refurbishment or internal redeployment before replacement. Compare repair/refurbishment costs with replacement costs and remaining useful life. Where equipment is no longer required, assess whether it can be reused or refurbished before treating it as waste. For genuine WEEE, use appropriate authorised collection/treatment routes and maintain records of equipment reused, refurbished and recycled.
KPI: Asset life: average equipment lifespan/years extended. Reuse: % of equipment repaired, refurbished or redeployed rather than replaced. Financial: £ avoided replacement expenditure. Carbon: tCO₂e avoided versus purchasing new equipment. WEEE: tonnes/% of end-of-life electrical equipment sent to appropriate reuse/recovery/recycling routes.
Sector_Included: All – particularly relevant for equipment-intensive operations such as hotels, contract caterers, breweries and restaurants
Source_Old_Initiative: Adopt a Circular approach for Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE)

Initiative_Name: Set responsible sourcing standards for packaging procurement
Description: Establish procurement standards that prioritise packaging made from responsibly sourced, recycled or renewable materials and that is designed for recyclability, while maintaining food safety, product quality and regulatory compliance.
Why_Benefit: Responsible packaging procurement can reduce reliance on virgin materials, improve traceability and support more sustainable material supply chains. Certification can provide evidence that materials such as paper and cardboard originate from responsibly managed or recycled sources, while designing for recyclability can also reduce exposure to higher UK EPR fees.
How_Text: Review packaging procurement specifications and establish minimum sustainability requirements by material. Require suppliers to provide evidence of material composition, recycled content and responsible sourcing, using recognised certification such as FSC for relevant paper/cardboard packaging. Include recyclability requirements in specifications and use the UK's Recyclability Assessment Methodology (RAM) where applicable. Review supplier compliance and update requirements as better packaging options become available.
KPI: Responsible sourcing: % of applicable packaging with recognised responsible-sourcing certification. Supplier compliance: % of packaging suppliers meeting procurement standards. Recyclability: % of packaging rated Green under RAM where applicable. Materials: % recycled/renewable content. Improvement: tonnes/% of non-compliant or poorly recyclable packaging replaced.
Sector_Included: All
Source_Old_Initiative: Opt for sustainably produced products made using eco-conscious methods and reclaimed materials

Initiative_Name: Procure lower-impact staff uniforms and operational textiles
Description: Procure uniforms, linen, towels and other operational textiles with lower lifecycle impacts by prioritising durability, responsible or recycled materials, repairability, reuse and appropriate end-of-life recovery.
Why_Benefit: Textiles contribute to Scope 3 emissions through raw material production, manufacturing and end-of-life treatment. Selecting durable, lower-impact textiles and extending their useful life can reduce demand for virgin materials, avoid replacement purchases and reduce textile waste and associated carbon emissions.
How_Text: Review procurement specifications for uniforms, linen, towels and other high-volume textiles. Prioritise durable products containing recycled or responsibly sourced fibres and request recognised certification where relevant, such as GOTS, GRS, OEKO-TEX or FSC for applicable fibres/materials. Include durability and repairability criteria in tenders, avoid unnecessary replacement, and establish systems to collect, repair, reuse, redistribute or recycle textiles at end of use.
KPI: Sustainable procurement: % of textile purchases meeting defined sustainability standards. Recycled/responsible content: % by weight. Asset life: average lifespan/replacement frequency of uniforms and linen. Reuse: % of textiles repaired/reused/redeployed. Waste: kg/tonnes of textiles diverted from disposal. Carbon: kg/tCO₂e avoided through reuse or lower-impact procurement.
Sector_Included: All – particularly relevant for hotels, restaurants, pubs/bars and contract caterers with high volumes of uniforms, linen and towels
Source_Old_Initiative: New Initiative

Initiative_Name: Procure environmentally preferable cleaning products
Description: Procure effective cleaning products with lower environmental impacts by considering chemical formulation, concentration and dosing, packaging, refillability and recognised environmental certification.
Why_Benefit: Environmentally preferable cleaning products can reduce chemical and packaging use, waste and associated environmental impacts. Concentrated and refillable systems can also reduce the volume of product purchased, transported and stored, while accurate dosing can prevent overuse and unnecessary cost.
How_Text: Review high-volume cleaning products and identify opportunities to switch to concentrated, refillable or lower-impact alternatives. Prioritise products carrying credible environmental certifications, such as the EU Ecolabel, where appropriate. Introduce controlled dosing or dilution systems for concentrates, work with suppliers to reduce packaging and increase refill/reuse, and train staff to use the correct product and dose while maintaining required hygiene and food-safety standards.
KPI: Procurement: % of cleaning spend/products meeting defined environmental criteria. Chemical use: litres/kg of cleaning concentrate used per room, cover or m² cleaned. Packaging: kg/number of cleaning-product containers avoided. Cost: £ cleaning-product cost per room/cover/m². Dosing: % correct dosing/compliance.
Sector_Included: All – particularly relevant for hotels, restaurants, pubs/bars, contract caterers and other operations with high cleaning-product use
Source_Old_Initiative: New initiative

Initiative_Name: Reduce office paper use and office consumables
Description: Reduce unnecessary paper and office consumable use by prioritising digital processes, controlling printing and procuring recycled or lower-impact products where physical materials remain necessary.
Why_Benefit: Reducing paper and consumable use lowers purchasing and printing costs, reduces waste and decreases the environmental impacts associated with paper production, toner, printing and disposal. Digital workflows can also improve document accessibility and administrative efficiency.
How_Text: Replace paper-based processes with digital documentation, e-signatures and electronic workflows where practical. Set printers to double-sided and black-and-white by default, introduce secure/pull printing where appropriate, monitor print volumes and remove unnecessary printers. Where printing remains necessary, procure recycled paper and lower-impact office consumables and track usage against a baseline.

How_Text: Begin by analysing travel data to identify key emissions hotspots, then establish a clear travel hierarchy that prioritises virtual meetings, rail, public transport, and low-emission vehicles before air travel. Initiative_Name: Provide infrastructure and incentives for low-carbon guest travel
Description: Providing the physical facilities and financial or practical incentives that make it easier for guests to travel to, from, and around a venue using lower carbon transport, rather than defaulting to private car or taxi use.
Why_Benefit: Guest travel is often one of the largest contributors to an organisation's overall carbon footprint, yet it is typically one of the hardest parts for a business to influence directly. Infrastructure and incentives are valuable precisely because they give businesses a genuine, controllable lever over this otherwise indirect source, EV charging points, shuttle services, and rewards for car-free travel all sit within the business's own decisions, rather than depending on guest behaviour alone. Beyond reducing emissions, these measures can enhance the guest experience, attract environmentally conscious customers, and create a competitive advantage that supports both sustainability and commercial objectives. EV charging in particular can generate direct revenue through session-based charging fees, alongside indirect revenue through increased bookings and occupancy from guests who specifically seek out charging access, turning the initiative into a commercial asset rather than a pure cost.
How_Text: The approach should be tailored to the site type. Businesses with control over their premises can install EV charging, cycle storage, and public transport signage. Those in leased locations can work with landlords to improve facilities and promote existing transport links. Rural sites may benefit from car-sharing schemes and partnerships with local taxi or shuttle providers, while hotels can offer shared transfers to reduce individual journeys. Infrastructure should be supported by incentives, such as discounts for car-free arrivals or priority access to EV charging, to encourage uptake and maximise impact.

Initiative_Name: Reduce emissions from delivery and distribution by improving fleet efficiency before the journey
How_Text:
1. Load & Route Planning: Right-size vehicles to actual load, and plan routes and loads together using route planning software or a logistics provider that sequences stops efficiently.
2. Shared Logistics: Explore haulage aggregation with other businesses, sharing truck space and routes so vehicles carry more, more often.
3. Vehicle Transition: Transition fleet to EVs or low-carbon fuel vehicles at natural end of service life, not early replacement, and install EV charging infrastructure at depots to support this.
4. Temperature controlled goods: Optimise cold chain and refrigerated transport, minimising stops and door-open time, consolidating loads, and prioritising electric or cryogenic refrigeration units over diesel.
5. Drive behaviour: Train drivers in smooth acceleration, reduced idling, and consistent route adherence.
Source_Old_Initiative:

Initiative_Name: Reduce emissions from delivery and distribution by improving fleet efficiency during and after the journey
How_Text:
1. Return Journey: Use the return journey for backhauling, carrying recycling, reusable packaging, or containers back to source rather than running empty.
2. Vehicle Monitoring: Install telematics and a digital asset management system to track fuel use, idling time, and vehicle condition in real time, and feed this data back into fleet decisions to catch maintenance issues early.
3. Delivery Timing: Schedule deliveries to avoid road congestion, ideally paired with route optimisation software.
Source_Old_Initiative: Backhaul recycling waste

Initiative_Name: Reduce emissions from delivery and distribution by engaging with suppliers
How_Text:
1. Procurement Consolidation: Centralise procurement across sites through a single system or department, consolidating orders to reduce delivery frequency, and favour suppliers offering efficient local delivery.
2. Supplier Engagement: Strengthen supplier relationship management, using regular engagement to request consolidated deliveries, emissions data, or lower-carbon transport options directly.
3. Delivery Consolidation: Ask suppliers to consolidate your deliveries with other nearby customers on the same route, rather than sending a dedicated part-load.
4. Order Timing: Apply just-in-time delivery principles with caution, balanced against consolidation, since tightly-timed delivery can increase emissions by disrupting efficient routing.
5. Demand Forecasting: Use data analytics to forecast demand and track supplier performance, reducing both waste and emissions-heavy urgent orders.

Initiative_Name: Reduce emissions from customer delivery
